questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic of the animal cell?

options.B: Possession of a cellulose cell wall

questions.explanation: Animal cells only have small, scattered vacuoles (unlike plant cells, which have one large permanent central vacuole). Chloroplasts and cellulose cell walls belong to plant cells, and chromosomes/genetic material are present in the cells of all living organisms, so they cannot be used to distinguish animal cells specifically.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: All living organisms
questions.explanation: Respiration (the release of energy from food) is a life process common to every living organism, plant or animal. Photosynthesis is restricted to green plants and some bacteria/algae; visible movement, feeding, and transpiration are not shown by every organism (e.g. plants do not "feed" the way animals do, and transpiration is a plant-specific water loss process).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The vacuole of a plant cell is

options.B: smaller than that of an animal cell

questions.explanation: The plant cell vacuole is bounded by a special membrane called the tonoplast, which controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell sap it contains. It is not empty (it is filled with cell sap, not air or a vacuum), and it is actually much larger than an animal cell's vacuole, not smaller.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The part of the cell solely responsible for respiration is the
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration, where energy stored in food is converted to ATP through the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. This is why mitochondria are nicknamed the "powerhouse of the cell." The other organelles listed have entirely different functions (heredity, ribosome production, packaging/secretion, and transport respectively).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of these combinations is common to plant and animal cells?

options.A: Centriole, middle lamella, Golgi bodies, mitochondrion
options.B: Cytoplasm, sap vacuole, starch grains, leucoplasts
options.D: Nucleus, nucleolus, cellulose cell wall, endoplasmic reticulum
options.E: Cytoplasm, centriole, cellulose cell wall, nucleolus

questions.explanation: Plasma membrane, chromosomes, mitochondria, and lysosomes are found in both plant and animal cells. Centrioles are normally absent in higher plant cells, cellulose cell walls and starch grains/leucoplasts and sap vacuoles are plant-specific features, so any option containing these cannot be "common to both."

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Where is energy produced in a cell?
questions.explanation: Energy (in the form of ATP) is generated in the mitochondria during aerobic respiration. The nucleus controls heredity, the nucleolus makes ribosomes, lysosomes digest materials, and chloroplasts trap light energy for photosynthesis (a different process from respiration, which releases energy).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following cell constituents is NOT common to both plants and animals?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are the organelles responsible for photosynthesis and are found only in plant cells (and some protists), never in animal cells. Mitochondria, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus, and (small) vacuoles are present in both plant and animal cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A group of similar cells performing the same function is
questions.explanation: This is the definition of a tissue — a collection of similar cells working together to perform a specific function (e.g. muscle tissue). An organ is made of different tissues working together; a system is made of organs; an organelle is a structure inside a single cell; an enzyme is a biological catalyst, not a cell grouping at all.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The function of endoplasmic reticulum is

options.C: digestion and destruction of foreign bodies

questions.explanation: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) forms a network of membranes/channels that transports materials (proteins, lipids) around inside the cell. Protein synthesis itself is carried out by ribosomes (which may be attached to the rough ER), digestion of foreign material is done by lysosomes, and energy production from glucose happens in the mitochondria.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The oxidative part of the respiration process takes place in the
questions.explanation: The oxidative stages of respiration (the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation/electron transport chain, which both require oxygen) occur inside the mitochondria. Only the very first, non-oxidative stage (glycolysis) occurs outside the mitochondria, in the cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The function of ribosomes in cells is
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are the cell structures where amino acids are joined together to form proteins (translation of mRNA). They play no role in starch synthesis, general material transport (that is the ER's job), or lipid storage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following structures is common to Euglena, white blood cell and Amoeba?
questions.explanation: A cell (surface) membrane is a universal feature of all cells, including Euglena, white blood cells, and Amoeba. Cell walls are absent in all three (they are all "naked" cells without a rigid wall), cilia are not a defining shared feature here, and while contractile vacuoles occur in Euglena and Amoeba, white blood cells do not have one.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which structure is known as the "power house" of the cell?
questions.explanation: Position 4 represents the mitochondrion, universally nicknamed the "powerhouse of the cell" because it is the main site of ATP (energy) production through aerobic respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following structures is associated with aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: The structure labelled 1 in the diagram represents the mitochondrion, the organelle where the oxygen-requiring (aerobic) stages of respiration take place.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The organelle involved in tissue respiration is the
questions.explanation: "Tissue respiration" refers to the cellular process of releasing energy from food, which takes place in the mitochondrion — this organelle contains the enzymes for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A tissue can best be defined as

options.B: an aggregate of cells performing a similar function
options.C: an aggregate of similar cells performing the same function
options.D: a mixture of different cell types performing the same function

questions.explanation: The precise biological definition of a tissue requires the cells to be similar (alike in structure/origin) AND working together to perform one common function — option C captures both conditions, while the other options are either too vague or describe a mixture of different cell types, which would actually describe an organ, not a tissue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The membrane surrounding the vacuole in a plant cell is called the
questions.explanation: The specific membrane that encloses the central vacuole and its cell sap in a plant cell is called the tonoplast. The plasmalemma is the outer cell surface membrane, and the other two options refer to entirely different structures (nucleus and cytoplasmic membrane network).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following organelles are likely to be present in cells that are actively respiring and photosynthesizing?
questions.explanation: Respiration occurs in mitochondria and photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, so a cell actively doing both (e.g. a green leaf mesophyll cell in daylight) would show large numbers of both organelles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The nucleus is considered the control organelle of a cell because it

options.C: is bounded by the nuclear membrane
options.D: is located at the centre of the cell

questions.explanation: The nucleus controls all cell activities because it houses the DNA (chromatin/genetic material), which carries the coded instructions for making proteins and regulating every cell process. The nuclear membrane, nuclear sap, and central position are structural features, not the reason it exercises control.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The structure that is most commonly identified in all living cells under the light microscope is the
questions.explanation: The nucleus is large and stains densely, making it the most easily seen and identified structure in cells under an ordinary light microscope. Mitochondria and ribosomes are generally too small to resolve clearly with a light microscope, and chloroplasts are absent from animal cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is an organ?
questions.explanation: The liver is a distinct organ made up of different tissues (epithelial, connective, vascular, etc.) working together for a common overall function. A guard cell is a single cell, a xylem bundle/vessel is a tissue, and blood is a (liquid connective) tissue, not an organ.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In plant cells, the chloroplasts are located
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are cytoplasmic organelles — they float within the cytoplasm of the cell (which itself lies inside the cell wall), not inside the vacuole and not outside the living protoplasm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following organisms does not exist as a single free-living cell?
questions.explanation: Volvox is a colonial organism — many individual cells are grouped together to form a hollow ball-shaped colony, so a single Volvox cell does not normally live independently. Paramecium, Amoeba, and Chlamydomonas are all true free-living unicellular organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An Amoeba and an unlaid chicken egg are
questions.explanation: Both an Amoeba and an unfertilized/unlaid chicken egg (the ovum) consist of just one single cell, even though the chicken egg cell is unusually large. Neither is a tissue (many cells), an organelle (a sub-cellular structure), nor, on its own, a fully developed multicellular organism.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The structures found only in plant cells are
questions.explanation: A cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts are structures unique to plant cells (and are absent from typical animal cells). Cell membrane, cytoplasm, chromatin, nucleolus, and lysosomes are all found in both plant and animal cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The rods in the retina of the eye are examples of
questions.explanation: Rods (like cones) are individual photoreceptor cells found in the retina that detect light. They are single specialized cells, not a tissue, organ, or system on their own.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The organelle common to both plant and animal cell is
questions.explanation: The plasmalemma (cell surface/plasma membrane) is present in every living cell, plant or animal. Centrioles are typically absent in higher plants, while cell walls and chloroplasts are plant-specific structures absent in animal cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is likely to have a higher concentration of mitochondria?
questions.explanation: A sperm cell needs a large amount of energy to power the whip-like movement of its tail as it swims through the female reproductive tract to reach the egg, so its mid-piece is packed with mitochondria. Mature red blood cells in mammals actually lack mitochondria (and even a nucleus) entirely.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The role of the Golgi complex in a eukaryotic cell is to

options.A: conduct ions in and out of the cell
options.B: transport genetic material out of the cell
options.D: transport organic material in and out of the cell

questions.explanation: The Golgi complex (apparatus) processes, packages, and transports substances such as proteins and other organic materials, often forming secretory vesicles that move materials into or out of the cell. It does not conduct ions, move genetic material, or provide attachment sites for ribosomes (that is a function of rough ER).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The organelle responsible for heredity is
questions.explanation: In the diagram, part I represents the nucleus, which houses the chromosomes (DNA) and is therefore responsible for heredity — passing genetic information from one generation of cells to the next.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A characteristic that can possibly be shared by both living and non-living things is
questions.explanation: Both living and non-living things can increase in size — for example, a crystal or a stalactite can grow larger by adding material to its outer surface, even though it is not alive. However, this growth is purely additive from outside, unlike true biological growth (increase in biomass through internal assimilation of food), which is unique to living things and is why "increase in biomass" is not a shared characteristic. Locomotion (self-directed movement) and irritability (response to stimuli) are also hallmarks of life not shared with non-living matter.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The cell of an onion bulb can be differentiated from a cheek cell by the presence of
questions.explanation: An onion bulb cell is a plant cell and therefore possesses a rigid cellulose cell wall, which a human cheek (epithelial) cell lacks. Both cell types have a plasmalemma and a nucleus, and neither typically contains chloroplasts (onion bulb cells store food but are not photosynthetic; cheek cells are animal cells).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: What is the level of organization of an onion bulb?
questions.explanation: An onion bulb is not just a single organ — it is an entire underground shoot system (comprising the stem and fleshy leaf bases) combined with its root system, together forming a complete organism capable of independent growth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A characteristic exhibited by all living organisms is

options.C: the ability to move from one place to another
options.D: the ability to remove unwanted substances

questions.explanation: All living organisms must excrete — that is, remove metabolic waste products — to avoid the build-up of toxic substances. Not all organisms reproduce sexually (many reproduce asexually), not all respire aerobically (some respire anaerobically), and not all organisms are capable of locomotion (e.g. plants are fixed in place).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a cell, the genes are carried by
questions.explanation: Genes are segments of DNA, and DNA in the nucleus exists in the form of chromatin threads (DNA wound around histone proteins), which condense into visible chromosomes during cell division. The nuclear membrane simply encloses the nucleus, while lysosomes and mitochondria are unrelated organelles with digestive and respiratory roles respectively (mitochondria do carry a small separate DNA, but this is not what is being tested here).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following characterizes a mature plant cell?

options.A: The nucleus is pushed to the centre of the cell
options.B: The cell wall is made up of cellulose
options.C: The nucleus is small and irregular in shape
options.D: The cytoplasm fills up the entire cell space

questions.explanation: A defining feature of plant cells at every stage is a cell wall made of cellulose. As a plant cell matures, the large central vacuole actually enlarges and pushes the nucleus and a thin layer of cytoplasm to the edge of the cell (the opposite of options A and D), while the nucleus retains a normal defined shape.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the nucleus of a cell?

options.A: It translates genetic information for the manufacture of proteins
options.B: It stores and carries hereditary information
options.C: It is a reservoir of energy for the cell
options.D: It controls the life processes of the cell

questions.explanation: Storing and releasing energy is the job of the mitochondrion, not the nucleus. The nucleus does store hereditary information (DNA), directs protein manufacture by sending instructions (mRNA) to the ribosomes, and generally controls the cell's activities.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The organelles present in cells that are actively respiring and photosynthesizing are
questions.explanation: As established earlier, respiration takes place in mitochondria and photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts, so an actively respiring and photosynthesizing cell (such as a leaf cell in sunlight) will be rich in both organelles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The lowest level of organization in living organisms is
questions.explanation: The hierarchy of biological organization runs from cell → tissue → organ → system → organism, in increasing order of complexity. The cell is therefore the most basic (lowest) level of organization that can still be considered a complete living unit.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is the most complex according to their cellular level of organization?
questions.explanation: The heart is a full organ, built from several different tissue types (muscle, connective, nervous, vascular) working together — this makes it the most complex option listed. Hair is simpler tissue-level material, Euglena is a single-celled organism, and although Hydra is a whole organism, its body organization does not progress beyond the tissue level, so it remains simpler than a true organ like the heart.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following organisms is multicellular?
questions.explanation: Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga made up of a chain of many cells joined end to end, making it multicellular. Chlamydomonas, Amoeba, and Euglena are all single-celled (unicellular) organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A Spirogyra cell was placed in solution X. After 1 minute the cell had been plasmolysed. Solution X was
questions.explanation: Plasmolysis (shrinking of the cell contents away from the cell wall) happens when a plant cell loses water to its surroundings by osmosis. This only occurs when the cell is placed in a strongly hypertonic solution — that is, a solution with a much higher solute concentration (much lower water potential) than the cell sap, such as a very strong sugar solution. Tap water, weak solutions, and distilled water are all more dilute than cell sap and would cause water to move into the cell instead.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration is
questions.explanation: This is the standard definition of diffusion — the net movement of any type of molecule (not just water) from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated, down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is a special case of diffusion that applies specifically to water across a semi-permeable membrane; the other terms describe unrelated processes (water loss from leaves, movement of food in phloem, and cell shrinkage).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A fresh kolanut weighing 1g was put into a salt solution. After 3 hours, the kolanut weighed 1.2g. This simple experiment demonstrates that

options.A: the salt solution is more concentrated than the cell sap of the kolanut
options.B: the cell sap of the kolanut is more concentrated than the salt solution
options.C: the salt solution has the same concentration as the cell sap of the kolanut
options.D: kolanut cells can multiply in water
options.E: the kolanut lost some water molecules to the salt solution

questions.explanation: Since the kolanut gained mass (from 1g to 1.2g), it must have absorbed water from the salt solution by osmosis. Water moves into a cell only when the surrounding solution is more dilute (has a higher water potential) than the cell's own contents — meaning the kolanut's cell sap was more concentrated (more negative water potential) than the salt solution around it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The filaments of Spirogyra were put into equal volumes of sugar solutions X and Y. After 5 minutes, filaments from solution X had their cell contents rounded up, while those from Y were unaffected. The experiment shows that

options.A: solution X was stronger than Y
options.B: solution Y was stronger than X
options.C: Spirogyra used up the sugar in solution Y
options.D: solution X is good for stimulating sexual reproduction in Spirogyra
options.E: solution Y was less contaminated than X

questions.explanation: Cell contents "rounding up" and pulling away from the cell wall is a classic sign of plasmolysis, which is caused by a strongly hypertonic (concentrated) external solution drawing water out of the cell. Since only the filaments in solution X plasmolysed, solution X must have been more concentrated ("stronger") than solution Y, which was too dilute to cause any visible water loss.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: If an isolated living cell is left in distilled water for two hours, it is likely to

options.A: lose some of its water to the surrounding water
options.B: lose all of its water to the surrounding water

questions.explanation: Distilled water is extremely hypotonic (has no solutes, so it has a very high water potential) compared to the cell's contents, so water will move into the cell by osmosis. If the cell in question is a plant cell, its rigid cellulose cell wall resists the resulting internal pressure, so instead of bursting, the cell simply becomes firm and swollen — that is, it becomes turgid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following will NOT allow osmosis to take place?
questions.explanation: Osmosis can only occur across a semi-permeable (partially permeable) membrane — one that lets small molecules like water pass through but not larger solute molecules. Pig's bladder, cellophane, parchment paper, and cow's bladder are all naturally semi-permeable. Transparent polythene, however, is completely impervious — it does not allow any molecules through at all — so no osmosis can take place across it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: When a Spirogyra cell is immersed in a salt solution more concentrated than its cell sap, it
questions.explanation: A salt solution that is more concentrated than the cell sap is hypertonic to the cell, meaning it has a lower water potential. Water will therefore move out of the Spirogyra cell into the salt solution by osmosis, causing the cell to lose water and shrivel (plasmolyse).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Osmosis can be defined as the movement of

options.A: molecules from a solution of high concentration to low concentration
options.B: molecules from a solution of low concentration to high concentration
options.C: water from a solution of high concentration to low concentration
options.D: water across a semi-permeable membrane from a solution of low (solute) concentration to high (solute) concentration
options.E: water across a semi-permeable membrane from a solution of high (solute) concentration to low (solute) concentration

questions.explanation: Osmosis is specifically the movement of water (not solute molecules in general) across a semi-permeable membrane, and it moves from a region where the solute concentration is low (and water potential is high) toward a region where the solute concentration is high (and water potential is low). This precise combination of conditions — water only, semi-permeable membrane, and direction relative to solute concentration — is exactly what option D describes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Mineral salts can be absorbed into the roots by
questions.explanation: Mineral salts (being solutes, not water) cannot be taken up by osmosis, which applies only to water. Instead, roots absorb mineral salts partly by diffusion (when soil solution concentration is higher outside than inside the root hair) and, importantly, by active transport, which uses metabolic energy (ATP from respiration) to move ions into the root even against their concentration gradient.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: After 30 minutes, the level of sugar solution in the set-up above will

options.C: be the same in X and Y

questions.explanation: Based on the diagram in the source text, set-up Y is arranged so that water can move by osmosis from the surrounding dilute water, through the semi-permeable membrane, into the more concentrated sugar solution — causing the solution level in Y to rise as it gains volume. In set-up X, the conditions given do not favour a net inward movement of water, so its level does not rise in the same way.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The process by which water moves from X to Y through the semi-permeable membrane is called
questions.explanation: Any movement of water (specifically) across a semi-permeable membrane, from a region of higher water potential to one of lower water potential, is by definition osmosis — regardless of which particular set-up or diagram it is shown in.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The process by which a red blood cell placed in distilled water absorbs water until it bursts and releases its contents into the surroundings is known as
questions.explanation: A red blood cell has no cell wall, so when placed in distilled water it takes in water by osmosis (a hypotonic environment) and keeps swelling until its membrane ruptures. This specific bursting of red blood cells due to excessive water uptake has its own special name: haemolysis. (Osmosis is the general water-movement process involved, but "haemolysis" is the more precise term for what happens to the cell itself.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Salts and water are absorbed in the roots and transported to the leaves by
questions.explanation: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis and is then transported upward through the xylem tissue (in a continuous transpiration stream) to the leaves, carrying dissolved mineral salts along with it by mass flow. The phloem, in contrast, transports manufactured food (like sugars), not water absorbed from the soil.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Yam is used in this set-up because it

options.A: is permeable to the salt solution

questions.explanation: The living tissue of the yam (like other plant tissues, e.g. pawpaw) behaves as a natural semi-permeable membrane, allowing water to pass through by osmosis while holding back the dissolved salt — this is exactly the property needed to demonstrate osmosis in this classic set-up.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following results is to be expected if the set-up is left for several hours?

options.A: decrease in the size of the yam cup
options.B: movement of the salt solution into the surrounding water
options.C: decrease in the volume of the surrounding water
options.D: movement of water from the salt solution into the surrounding dish

questions.explanation: Because the salt solution inside the yam cup is more concentrated (hypertonic) than the water in the surrounding dish, water moves by osmosis out of the dish and into the yam cup, through the semi-permeable yam tissue. Over several hours this causes a noticeable decrease in the volume of water remaining in the outer dish, while the salt solution level inside the yam cup rises.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A marine protozoan is unlikely to have a contractile vacuole mainly because its cytoplasm is
questions.explanation: A contractile vacuole exists to pump out excess water that continually enters a cell by osmosis. If a marine protozoan's cytoplasm is isotonic with (has the same solute concentration as) the surrounding seawater, there is no net osmotic gain of water, so the organism has no need to actively expel excess water and can manage without a contractile vacuole.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following can cause shrinkage of living cells?
questions.explanation: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration (lower water potential) than the cell's contents, so it draws water out of the cell by osmosis (ex-osmosis), causing the cell to shrink. Deionized/distilled water and hypotonic solutions instead cause cells to gain water and swell, while isotonic solutions cause no net water movement at all.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Euglena may be classified as a plant because it
questions.explanation: The possession of chloroplasts (allowing Euglena to photosynthesize like a plant) is its key plant-like feature. Its gullet, pellicle, and flagellum are actually animal-like features (since it also lacks a cellulose cell wall), and living in a pond is simply a habitat, not a classification criterion.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Rhizopus (or Mucor) obtains its food from dead organic matter extracellularly. It is said to be
questions.explanation: An organism that feeds on dead and decaying organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes onto it and absorbing the digested products (extracellular digestion) is called a saprophyte. Parasites feed on living hosts, commensals live alongside another organism without harming or feeding directly off its tissue in this way, and autotrophs manufacture their own food.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which one of the following options is not true for Mucor or Rhizopus?

options.A: grows on moist dead organic matter

questions.explanation: Fungal cell walls (including those of Mucor/Rhizopus) are made of chitin, not cellulose, so option C is the false statement being tested here. (It is worth noting that, by modern classification, fungi are no longer classified as plants at all — they form their own separate kingdom — but at the time this question was set, "is a plant" was still treated as broadly acceptable, so chitin-versus-cellulose is the specific error intended.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: One of the following statements is not true of viruses.

options.C: They can be seen with an ordinary light microscope

questions.explanation: Viruses are far too small to be seen with an ordinary light microscope — they can only be observed using an electron microscope, which has much higher magnifying and resolving power. Viruses are indeed microscopic, smaller than bacteria, and can cause plant diseases such as tobacco mosaic disease.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: In Mucor or Rhizopus, carbohydrate is absorbed in the form of
questions.explanation: Like other fungi, Mucor digests complex carbohydrates extracellularly into the simplest absorbable sugar, glucose, before taking it up into its hyphae. Once inside, this glucose is then converted and stored in a different form (see the next question).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: In Rhizopus, carbohydrate is stored in the form of
questions.explanation: After absorbing glucose, fungi such as Rhizopus convert and store their carbohydrate reserves as glycogen — the same storage carbohydrate used by animal cells — rather than as starch (used by plants) or paramylum (used by Euglena).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: In which of the following groups of animals are flagella and cilia found?
questions.explanation: The phylum Protozoa contains members that move by different means — for example, Amoeba by pseudopodia, Paramecium by cilia, and Euglena/Chlamydomonas by flagella — so both flagella and cilia are found within this one group, in different species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true of Mucor?

options.C: it bears spores in a sporangium

questions.explanation: Mucor is a fungus, and fungi lack chlorophyll entirely (they cannot photosynthesize and must obtain food from organic sources). It does grow saprophytically, has a hyphal body, produces spores in a sporangium, and can reproduce sexually by conjugation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Viruses are regarded as non-living because they

options.A: can neither reproduce asexually nor sexually
options.B: cannot survive in their respective environments
options.C: do not possess characteristics that can be transmitted from one generation to the next

questions.explanation: Respiration and excretion are basic metabolic activities carried out independently by every true living cell. Viruses have no cellular machinery of their own to carry out these processes — they rely entirely on a host cell's machinery even to replicate — which is a major reason they are often classified as non-living outside a host.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following features of Euglena is found only in animals?
questions.explanation: A pellicle (a flexible protein-based outer covering, used instead of a rigid cell wall) is a distinctly animal-like feature of Euglena. Paramylum granules and pyrenoids are associated with its plant-like carbohydrate/starch storage, and flagella are found in both plant-like and animal-like organisms, so they are not exclusively animal features.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The hypha of Rhizopus is said to be coenocytic because it
questions.explanation: "Coenocytic" (or aseptate) describes a hypha that is one continuous tube of cytoplasm containing many nuclei, without internal cross-walls (septa) dividing it into separate cells. This lack of cross walls is exactly what the term coenocytic refers to.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Spirogyra, Euglena and Chlamydomonas share many characteristics EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Spirogyra is a non-motile filamentous alga — it cannot actively move from place to place — whereas both Euglena and Chlamydomonas are motile, propelling themselves using flagella. All three, however, share similarities in their nutrition (photosynthetic), modes of reproduction, and general irritability (response to stimuli).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: What is the function of trichocyst in Paramecium?
questions.explanation: Trichocysts are small organelles just beneath the cell surface of Paramecium that can rapidly discharge thread-like filaments to the outside. This discharge is used mainly for defence against predators (and sometimes to help anchor the organism), not for movement (which is the job of cilia), excretion (contractile vacuole), or reproduction (which involves the nuclei).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: When a virus is placed in a non-living medium, it
questions.explanation: Outside a living host, a virus can become inactive and form a crystal-like structure, remaining in this non-living crystalline state until it once again enters a suitable host cell, at which point it "reactivates" and resumes its living, infective characteristics.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: A multinucleate body without internal cell boundaries is characteristic of
questions.explanation: This describes the coenocytic hyphae of many fungi (such as Rhizopus/Mucor) — a single continuous mass of cytoplasm containing many nuclei but no internal walls separating them into distinct cells, unlike bryophytes, algae, or gymnosperms, whose bodies are made of separate, walled cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Viruses are considered to be living organisms because they

options.B: move from one place to another

questions.explanation: Every virus contains a core of genetic material — either DNA or RNA, never both — that carries coded hereditary information capable of being copied and passed on (transmitted) to new virus particles once inside a host cell. This capacity for heredity is the main reason they are sometimes considered to have a "living" characteristic, even though they lack most other features of life such as independent movement, response, or feeding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following characteristics is common to Amoeba and Paramecium?
questions.explanation: Both Amoeba and Paramecium are freshwater protozoans that constantly take in excess water by osmosis, so both possess a contractile vacuole to pump this excess water back out (osmoregulation). Oral grooves, trichocysts, and cilia, however, are specific to Paramecium and are not found in Amoeba.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following are non-green plants?
questions.explanation: Fungi completely lack chlorophyll and are therefore never green; they cannot photosynthesize at all. Euglena and Spirogyra both contain chlorophyll (green pigment) for photosynthesis, and angiosperms are flowering green plants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: One of the features which adapts Paramecium to its environment is the possession of
questions.explanation: Cilia allow Paramecium to swim actively — moving toward food sources and away from danger or unfavourable conditions — which is a key adaptation for a free-living organism in its watery environment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: In which of the following organisms does a single cell perform all the functions of movement, nutrition, growth, excretion and photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Euglena is unicellular, motile (by flagellum), and photosynthetic (it contains chlorophyll), so a single Euglena cell alone carries out movement, feeding, growth, excretion, and photosynthesis. Paramecium and Amoeba cannot photosynthesize, and Spirogyra, though photosynthetic, is technically a multicellular (filamentous) organism, not a single free cell.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The spores of mucor are dispersed by
questions.explanation: Mucor produces very light, dry spores inside a sporangium; once released, these spores are carried away by air currents (wind) and germinate into new fungal colonies wherever they land on a suitable substrate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Members of the phylum Protozoa use the contractile vacuole
questions.explanation: Freshwater protozoans constantly absorb water by osmosis because their surroundings are more dilute than their cytoplasm; the contractile vacuole collects this excess water and periodically expels it from the cell, preventing the cell from bursting.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE of the process of conjugation in Paramecium?
questions.explanation: During conjugation, two Paramecium cells pair up at their oral grooves and exchange micronuclear genetic material. Each micronucleus involved actually divides twice (through a meiotic-type process) to produce the necessary haploid nuclei for exchange, after which each ex-conjugant itself divides twice more, eventually giving rise to four daughter cells per original conjugant (eight cells in total from the pair).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The smallest living organisms which share the characteristics of both living and non-living matter are
questions.explanation: Viruses are the smallest biological entities known, and they display a mix of living traits (they carry genetic material capable of heredity) and non-living traits (no independent metabolism, growth, or reproduction outside a host cell) — which is why they are often described as sitting at the boundary between living and non-living matter.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following does a virus have in common with animal cells?
questions.explanation: Both viruses and animal cells contain nucleic acid as their genetic material — a virus contains either DNA or RNA, and animal cells contain DNA. However, viruses have no true nucleus, no cytoplasm, and do not store glycogen, unlike animal cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Viruses differ from all forms of life because they

options.B: feed on waste products of other organisms
options.D: require other living cells to multiply

questions.explanation: The defining biological limitation of a virus is that it cannot reproduce (multiply) on its own — it must invade a living host cell and hijack that cell's machinery in order to make copies of itself. Not all viruses cause disease, they do not have a "thick cell wall," and they certainly do not feed on waste products.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The procaryotic cell type is characterized by

options.A: a complex cytoplasm in which different regions are poorly defined
options.B: localization of different regions of the cell into tissues
options.C: a collection of organelles and macromolecular complexes

questions.explanation: Prokaryotic cells (like bacteria and blue-green algae/cyanobacteria) lack membrane-bound organelles, so their cytoplasm, while chemically complex and full of various molecular machinery, has no clearly compartmentalized regions the way a eukaryotic cell's organelles do. (Prokaryotic cells apply only to bacteria and cyanobacteria; all other organisms are eukaryotic.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The most recently evolved structure in animals is the
questions.explanation: Hair is a defining feature unique to mammals, which are considered the most recently evolved and most advanced class of vertebrates, sitting at the top of the evolutionary scale among the options given (scales belong to older groups like fish/reptiles, feathers to birds, and cilia are an ancient, primitive cellular structure).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The order in which organic evolution has progressed in plants is

options.A: Thallophyta, Schizophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta
options.B: Schizophyta, Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta
options.C: Pteridophyta, Spermatophyta, Thallophyta, Schizophyta and Bryophyta
options.D: Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Spermatophyta, Thallophyta and Schizophyta

questions.explanation: Plant evolution progressed from the simplest prokaryotic organisms upward: Schizophyta (bacteria and blue-green algae) → Thallophyta (algae) → Bryophyta (mosses/liverworts) → Pteridophyta (ferns) → Spermatophyta (seed-bearing plants), representing increasing structural complexity over time.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following groups is the most advanced?
questions.explanation: Gymnosperms are seed-bearing plants and represent a more advanced evolutionary stage than thallophytes (algae), bryophytes (mosses), or pteridophytes (ferns), none of which produce true seeds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The animals that move by means of flagella include
questions.explanation: Both Chlamydomonas and Euglena are flagellates — single-celled organisms that swim using one or more whip-like flagella. Amoeba moves by pseudopodia, Paramecium by cilia, and Planaria and Hydra move using muscular/ciliary means rather than flagella.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The umbrella-shaped fruiting body of a fully developed mushroom is the
questions.explanation: The pileus is the umbrella-shaped cap that sits on top of the mushroom's stalk (stipe); together, tightly packed hyphae form this cap and stalk structure. The mycelium is the underground/underlying network of hyphae, and the basidium is the microscopic spore-producing structure found on the gills beneath the cap, not the visible "umbrella" itself.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The similarity among organisms belonging to the same group will be least within each
questions.explanation: In taxonomic classification, kingdom is the broadest, most inclusive category, so members within the same kingdom can be extremely varied (e.g. a mushroom and a human are both in different kingdoms, but a fungus and a mould could be quite different within the same kingdom Fungi). Species, in contrast, is the narrowest classification, so members of the same species are the most alike.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The cell component that is present in a prokaryotic cell is the
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic cells (bacteria and cyanobacteria) lack membrane-bound organelles such as chloroplasts, mitochondria, and a true nuclear envelope, but they do contain ribosomes (specifically the smaller 70S type), which are essential for protein synthesis in every living cell.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: A plant-like feature in Euglena is the
questions.explanation: The pigment spot (eyespot/stigma) in Euglena is associated with its chloroplast and helps the organism detect and orient itself toward light for photosynthesis — a plant-like function. Pellicle and gullet, by contrast, are animal-like features.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The most common characteristic of the fungal hyphae is the possession of

options.A: cell-like compartments with one nucleus each
options.B: cell walls that are both rigid and chitinous
options.C: a multicellular mycelium in the substrate

questions.explanation: Fungal hyphal walls are consistently rigid and made of chitin (not cellulose), regardless of whether the hyphae are divided by cross-walls (septate) or not (aseptate/coenocytic) — making this the most universally common feature among fungal hyphae.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The hyphal wall of fungi is rigid owing to the presence of
questions.explanation: Chitin, a tough nitrogen-containing polysaccharide (the same substance found in insect exoskeletons), gives fungal hyphal walls their rigidity — not cellulose (found in plant cell walls) or lignin (a plant cell wall-strengthening compound).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The organelle responsible for sexual reproduction is
questions.explanation: The part labelled I in this diagram represents the micronucleus, which is exchanged between two conjugating Paramecium cells during sexual reproduction (conjugation) — the macronucleus, by contrast, controls everyday cell functions but plays no role in this genetic exchange.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The chromosomes of members of the kingdom Monera are within the
questions.explanation: Members of the kingdom Monera (bacteria and blue-green algae) are prokaryotic and have no true, membrane-bound nucleus. Their single circular chromosome lies free within the cytoplasm, in a region sometimes loosely called the nucleoid, rather than being enclosed by a nuclear membrane.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The process illustrated is
questions.explanation: The diagram depicts conjugation between two compatible hyphae of Rhizopus, ending in the formation of a zygospore — this is specifically sexual reproduction in Rhizopus, not in Spirogyra (which conjugates differently, via filament-to-filament tube formation).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: In terms of the number of individuals, which of the following taxa is most inclusive?
questions.explanation: Following the taxonomic hierarchy (Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species), class ranks higher than order, family, and species among the options given, meaning it contains the largest number of different individuals/organisms overall.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: A blue-green alga is not a protophyte because

options.D: it is not a green plant

questions.explanation: Protophytes (plant-like protists, e.g. true algae) are eukaryotic organisms. Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) are actually prokaryotic, like bacteria, which is why they are classified under the kingdom Monera rather than as protophytes, despite being photosynthetic and superficially algae-like.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following groups of cells is devoid of true nuclei?
questions.explanation: Members of the kingdom Monera (bacteria and cyanobacteria) are prokaryotic, meaning their genetic material is not enclosed within a true, membrane-bound nucleus. Algae and fungi are eukaryotic and do have true nuclei, and viruses are not made of cells at all, so this question is best answered with reference to actual cellular organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following is the lowest category of classification?
questions.explanation: Species is the most specific, narrowest, and lowest-ranking unit in the standard taxonomic hierarchy, sitting below genus, family, order, and class.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The fungi are a distinct group of eukaryotes mainly because they have
questions.explanation: While fungi do lack chlorophyll, this alone doesn't distinguish them (animal cells also lack chlorophyll), and spores plus sexual/asexual reproduction are shared with other groups like bryophytes and protozoans. What is genuinely distinctive about fungi is their characteristic fruiting bodies built from a mass of branching hyphae (mycelium) — a structural feature unique to this kingdom.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: The organ which is sensitive to light in Euglena is
questions.explanation: The eyespot (stigma) is a light-sensitive pigmented structure near the base of the flagellum in Euglena, allowing the organism to detect light direction and swim toward well-lit areas for effective photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Which of the following is the simplest living organism?
questions.explanation: If a virus is considered to be "alive" for the purposes of this question, then it is structurally by far the simplest of the options, consisting of little more than genetic material wrapped in a protein coat, with no cell structure or organelles at all — far simpler than any of the true unicellular organisms listed. (It should be noted, however, that many biologists dispute whether viruses should be classed as "living" at all, precisely because of this lack of independent cellular machinery.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION I — VIRUSES, MONERA, PROTISTA, FUNGI
questions.question: Fungi are referred to as heterotrophs because they
questions.explanation: Without chlorophyll, fungi cannot photosynthesize and manufacture their own food the way green plants (autotrophs) do; instead, they must obtain organic nutrients from other sources (dead matter, hosts, or partners), which is the defining feature of a heterotroph.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The following events take place during conjugation in Spirogyra: (1) The protoplasm in each of the conjugating cells separates from the cell wall to form a gamete; the gamete of one filament passes through the conjugation tube to meet the gamete of the other filament (2) the zygote soon becomes surrounded by a thick brown wall to become a zygospore, which bursts after a short rest and germinates to produce a new filament (3) the nuclei of the gametes fuse to form a zygote (4) the protuberances meet and where they touch, the cell wall disappears so that a conjugation tube joining the two cells is formed (5) protuberances appear on the walls of cells of two filaments of Spirogyra lying side by side opposite one another. What is the correct sequence in which the above events occur?
questions.explanation: Conjugation logically must begin with two filaments lying side by side developing outward bulges (5 — protuberances appear), which then meet and fuse into a connecting bridge (4 — the conjugation tube forms). Only then can the cell contents round up into gametes and one gamete migrate across the tube to the other cell (1). Once united, the two gamete nuclei fuse to form a zygote (3), which finally develops a thick protective wall to become the resting zygospore (2). This gives the order 5, 4, 1, 3, 2.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: One of the following statements is Not true of Spirogyra

options.A: It is a simple multicellular plant
options.B: During conjugation, its gametes, which are structurally and physiologically similar, fuse to form a zygote
options.C: It possesses spiral chloroplast which enable the plant to photosynthesize
options.D: Its cells are protected externally by a layer of mucilage
options.E: There are pyrenoids along the chloroplast

questions.explanation: Although the gametes of Spirogyra look structurally identical (isogametes), they are not physiologically identical — one filament's gametes behave as the "male" (motile, moving through the conjugation tube) and the other's as the "female" (stays put, receives the other gamete), even though nothing about their shape or size distinguishes them. Calling them "physiologically similar" is therefore inaccurate, making B the false statement. Spirogyra genuinely is multicellular, has spiral ribbon-like chloroplasts with pyrenoids, and is coated in a slimy mucilage layer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: One common feature of the fungi, algae, mosses and ferns is that they
questions.explanation: None of these four groups (fungi, algae, mosses, ferns) produce true seeds — seed production is a feature of the more advanced spermatophytes (gymnosperms and angiosperms) only. Fungi are not photosynthetic, conjugation is specific to certain algae/fungi (not universal to all four), and alternation of generations, while present in algae/mosses/ferns, is not a defining feature of fungi.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which of the following represents the evolutionary sequence in these plants? (1) Flowering plants (2) Ferns (3) Mosses (4) Algae (5) Conifers
questions.explanation: Plant evolution runs from the simplest to the most advanced groups: algae (4) evolved first, followed by mosses (3), then ferns (2), then the seed-bearing conifers/gymnosperms (5), and finally the most advanced group, the flowering plants/angiosperms (1) — giving the sequence 4→3→2→5→1.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Mosses, liverworts and ferns can be grouped together because they
questions.explanation: Mosses, liverworts, and ferns all reproduce by spores rather than seeds, making "seedless plants" the shared feature that groups them together. They are not exclusively aquatic or desert plants, and ferns (unlike mosses/liverworts) do have differentiated roots, stems, and leaves — and none of them produce flowers at all.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Spirogyra and Mucor can be grouped together as Thallophyta because

options.B: their spores could be dispersed by wind
options.C: they are capable of living independent lives
options.E: their bodies are made up of thallus and filaments alternatively

questions.explanation: The defining feature of the group Thallophyta is that the plant body is a simple, undifferentiated "thallus" — which in the case of these particular organisms takes the form of simple filaments (Spirogyra's chain of cells, or Mucor's hyphal threads) rather than true roots, stems, and leaves. Neither organism is unicellular (both are filamentous/multicellular), and both can reproduce asexually as well as sexually.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which of the following is INCORRECT? The prothallus of a fern

options.B: is green because its cells contain chloroplasts
options.E: is attached to the ground by numerous rhizoids

questions.explanation: In ferns, it is the sporophyte (the familiar large leafy fern plant) that is the dominant, conspicuous generation — not the prothallus, which is a small, inconspicuous, short-lived gametophyte stage. The prothallus is indeed heart-shaped, green (photosynthetic), bears the sexual organs (antheridia and archegonia), and is anchored by rhizoids.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In Spirogyra, the Pyrenoid

options.E: makes the plant slimy to touch

questions.explanation: Pyrenoids are small protein-rich bodies attached to the spiral chloroplast of Spirogyra, and they function as centres where starch is synthesized and accumulated from the products of photosynthesis. (It is the nucleus, not the pyrenoid, that is suspended by cytoplasmic strands in the cell.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Bryophytes are different from flowering plants because they
questions.explanation: The single most fundamental difference is that bryophytes (mosses and liverworts) lack true vascular (conducting) tissues — xylem and phloem — which flowering plants possess. This absence of vascular tissue is exactly why bryophytes remain small and restricted to moist habitats, but the vascular tissue distinction itself is the defining, non-negotiable difference.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In lower plants like mosses, the structure which performs the functions of roots of higher plants is called
questions.explanation: Mosses have no true roots; instead, they anchor themselves to the substrate and absorb some water using thread-like structures called rhizoids, which perform a root-like anchoring function without possessing any true root tissue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true of Spirogyra?
questions.explanation: Spirogyra filaments are unbranched — they consist of a single chain of cylindrical cells joined end to end, never dividing into branches. Spirogyra does reproduce both sexually (by conjugation) and asexually (by fragmentation, where a broken piece of filament grows into a new filament).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In a plant exhibiting alternation of generations, the diploid multicellular stage is known as
questions.explanation: In the alternation-of-generations life cycle, the sporophyte is the diploid (2n) multicellular stage that produces spores by meiosis. The gametophyte, by contrast, is the haploid (n) stage that produces gametes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: A characteristic that distinguishes bryophytes from flowering plants is the

options.A: possession of true stems and leaves
options.D: ability to grow in moist habitats

questions.explanation: As with an earlier question in this set, the absence of vascular (conducting) tissue in bryophytes is the key structural distinction that separates them from flowering plants, which possess well-developed xylem and phloem.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In most true ferns, sporangia are grouped into
questions.explanation: Clusters of sporangia on the underside of a fern frond are grouped into structures called sori (singular: sorus). The indusium is simply the protective flap covering a sorus, the frond is the fern's leaf, and the prothallus is the separate gametophyte generation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In the reproduction of mosses, water is essential because

options.C: the male gametes must swim to fertilize the ovum

questions.explanation: Mosses have flagellated, swimming male gametes (antherozoids) that require a film of water to physically swim from the antheridium to the archegonium in order to fertilize the egg cell (ovum) — this is the specific reason water is essential for their sexual reproduction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The term 'Thallophyta' refers to
questions.explanation: Thallophyta is the traditional grouping for plant-like organisms whose bodies are a simple, undifferentiated thallus rather than true roots/stems/leaves — this classically includes the algae and the fungi.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The prothallus of a fern is equivalent to the gametophyte generation of a moss because it
questions.explanation: Both the fern prothallus and the moss's leafy gametophyte plant are the haploid generation responsible for producing the sexual organs (antheridia and archegonia) and the gametes — this shared reproductive role is what makes them functionally equivalent generations, even though the fern prothallus is comparatively far less conspicuous than the moss gametophyte.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes are similar in that they
questions.explanation: All three groups produce motile, swimming male gametes that need a film of external water to reach and fertilize the female gamete — so moisture is essential for fertilization across algae, bryophytes, and pteridophytes alike. (Note that pteridophytes, unlike bryophytes, do have vascular tissue, so B cannot be the shared feature.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The spores of ferns are dispersed by
questions.explanation: The sporangium wall of a fern includes a specialized ring of cells called the annulus, which builds up tension as it dries and eventually snaps back suddenly, catapulting the spores explosively away from the parent plant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In bryophytes, sex organs are produced in the
questions.explanation: The gametophyte generation (the familiar leafy moss plant or liverwort thallus) is the haploid stage responsible for bearing the sex organs — antheridia (male) and archegonia (female) — and producing the gametes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which of the following are differentiated into true roots, stems and leaves?
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes (ferns and their relatives) are the simplest plant group to possess true vascular tissue, and with it, genuinely differentiated roots, stems, and leaves — unlike algae, schizophytes (bacteria/blue-green algae), and bryophytes, all of which lack true vascular structures.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The annulus of fern sporangium helps in
questions.explanation: As explained earlier, the annulus is a ring of specialized thick-walled cells on the sporangium that dries out, builds tension, and then snaps to catapult the spores away — its role is entirely about aiding spore dispersal.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which of the following correctly summarizes the life cycle of a fern plant?
questions.explanation: A fern's life cycle correctly runs: the prothallus (gametophyte) produces a spermatozoid (male gamete) that swims to fertilize the egg cell (female gamete) in the archegonium; this fertilized egg then develops into the mature leafy fern plant (sporophyte), which eventually produces spores in its sporangia — matching the sequence given in option D.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In which of these features do bryophytes differ from pteridophytes?
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes (ferns) possess true vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), while bryophytes (mosses/liverworts) do not — this is the key structural difference between the two groups. Both groups lack flowers, both show alternation of generations, and both require water for the swimming male gametes to reach the egg.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which of the following organs or cell components are common to both the sporophyte and the gametophyte of a fern?
questions.explanation: Both the fern's sporophyte (the leafy plant) and its gametophyte (the prothallus) are photosynthetic and therefore contain chloroplasts in their cells. However, only the sporophyte has true roots and leaves, while only the prothallus has rhizoids (root-like anchoring structures, not true roots).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which is the correct order in an evolutionary sequence for the following plant groups?

options.D: Bacteria mosses algae ferns seed plants

questions.explanation: The evolutionary order of increasing complexity runs from the simplest prokaryotes (bacteria) through algae, then mosses, then ferns, and finally to the seed-bearing plants — matching option C exactly.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: One common characteristic of fungi, algae, mosses and ferns is that they
questions.explanation: All four groups reproduce using spores that are released and dispersed to form new individuals. Fungi lack chlorophyll (ruling out D), conjugation as a reproductive method is specific to certain algae and fungi rather than universal (ruling out B), and while alternation of generations occurs in algae/mosses/ferns, it is not a defining feature of fungi (ruling out A).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Which of the following perform similar functions?
questions.explanation: A sorus is a cluster of spore-producing sporangia on a fern frond, and the indusium is the protective covering flap over that same cluster — the two work together directly in the same structure and function (protecting and housing developing spores).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In ferns, the sporophyte

options.C: is haploid and dependent on the gametophyte
options.D: is diploid and independent of the gametophyte

questions.explanation: The fern sporophyte (the familiar leafy fern plant) develops from a diploid zygote, grows independently once established, and reproduces asexually by producing haploid spores (not sexually) — making D the accurate description.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In which of the following organisms does each cell combine the function of nutrition, reproduction and growth?
questions.explanation: Although Spirogyra is a filamentous (chain-like) alga, each individual cell within the filament is functionally independent and capable of carrying out nutrition, growth, and reproduction on its own (for example, any single cell can participate in conjugation or contribute to fragmentation), unlike the more differentiated, multicellular bodies of Rhizopus (a fungus), Dryopteris (a fern), or Brachymenium (a moss).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: In ferns, the structure above is equivalent to the
questions.explanation: The fern prothallus shown is the haploid gametophyte generation, bearing the sexual organs — functionally equivalent to the leafy gametophyte generation of a moss, which likewise bears the sex organs and produces the gametes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: One distinctive feature in the life history of liverworts is that they exhibit
questions.explanation: Like mosses and ferns, liverworts show a true alternation of generations between a haploid gametophyte stage and a diploid sporophyte stage — this is the most distinctive and defining feature of their life history, since asexual/vegetative/sexual reproduction individually are not unique to liverworts alone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The absence of special food and water-conducting systems restricts the body size in
questions.explanation: Algae, liverworts, and mosses all lack true vascular (conducting) tissue for transporting water and food efficiently over long distances, which limits how large their bodies can grow. Ferns (pteridophytes), by contrast, do possess vascular tissue and can therefore grow considerably larger.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The dominant phase in the life cycle of a bryophyte is the
questions.explanation: In bryophytes (mosses and liverworts), the gametophyte is the larger, longer-lived, and more conspicuous generation — the familiar green, leafy moss plant is itself the gametophyte, while the sporophyte remains small and dependent on it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: A water medium is necessary for fertilization in
questions.explanation: Ferns retain motile, swimming male gametes that require a film of water to reach the egg cell for fertilization, just as in mosses. Conifers and angiosperms, more evolutionarily advanced, use pollen (carried by wind or animals) rather than swimming gametes, so external water is no longer needed for their fertilization.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Alternation of asexual and sexual modes of reproduction is found in
questions.explanation: Ferns show a true alternation of generations, in which the sexually reproducing gametophyte (prothallus) generation alternates with the asexually spore-producing sporophyte (leafy fern) generation. Blue-green algae and Euglena reproduce mainly asexually, and maize (a flowering plant) reproduces only sexually via seeds, without a comparable alternating asexual spore-producing stage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: The dominant phase in the life cycle of a fern is the
questions.explanation: Unlike in bryophytes, in ferns it is the sporophyte (the large, leafy fern plant) that is the dominant, long-lived generation, while the gametophyte (prothallus) is small, short-lived, and much less conspicuous.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION II — PLANTAE: THALLOPHYTA, BRYOPHYTA, PTERIDOPHYTA
questions.question: Alternation of generation is a feature shown in
questions.explanation: Mosses (bryophytes) show a clear, textbook alternation of generations between a dominant haploid gametophyte and a dependent diploid sporophyte. Fungi, grasses, and conifers do not follow this same alternating pattern of two distinct, free-living generations in the same way.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The number shown as 8 refers to
questions.explanation: Based on the labelled leaf-section diagram in the source text, structure 8 corresponds to a guard cell — the specialized bean-shaped cell that borders and controls the opening (stoma) in the lower epidermis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The structure responsible for trapping the sun's energy during photosynthesis is
questions.explanation: Position 3 in the diagram corresponds to the palisade mesophyll layer — the tightly packed, chloroplast-rich cells directly beneath the upper epidermis that are the leaf's primary site for trapping light energy for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of these plays no role in photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Position 2 in the diagram represents the upper epidermis, whose cells lack chloroplasts and are transparent, existing purely to protect the leaf and let light through — they take no direct part in photosynthesis itself, unlike the guard cells, mesophyll layers, and stoma, which are all directly involved in gas exchange or light-trapping.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Root hairs have their origin from
questions.explanation: Root hairs are simply thin, tubular extensions of individual epidermal cells (specifically the outermost layer, also called the piliferous layer) of the root, formed to increase the surface area for water and mineral absorption.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: One significant difference between roots and stem is that

options.A: branch roots originate in the pericycle while branch stems do not
options.B: stems are always above the ground while roots are always below the ground
options.C: stems are positively geotropic while roots are negatively geotropic
options.D: stems are sometimes used for storage while roots are never so used
options.E: stems grow in both length and circumference while roots grow only in length

questions.explanation: Lateral (branch) roots arise internally from a specific tissue layer called the pericycle, deep within the root. Branch stems, by contrast, develop externally from axillary buds at the nodes, not from any internal pericycle-like tissue — this is a genuine structural distinction (the other listed statements are all factually incorrect: stems can be underground, roots can also be modified for storage, and both organs can thicken in girth).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following tissues are made up of dead cells?
questions.explanation: Mature xylem vessel elements and tracheids lose their living contents once fully developed, leaving behind hollow, lignified dead cell walls that form efficient water-conducting tubes. Meristematic and cambium tissues, by contrast, consist of actively dividing living cells, and mesophyll/palisade cells are living, photosynthetic cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Root hairs are developed from the
questions.explanation: As established earlier, root hairs are simple extensions of the outermost epidermal (piliferous) layer of a root, not from any of the internal vascular or meristematic tissues.

questions.subject: Biology
