questions.question: Which of the following features can be used to identify Fig. 1 (as a stem rather than a root)?
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, part 3 represents a tissue (such as pith arrangement or vascular bundle pattern) that is characteristic of stem anatomy and absent (or arranged differently) in root cross-sections, making its presence the identifying clue for this being a dicot stem.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The main function of 6 is to

options.E: conduct carbon dioxide to the other parts

questions.explanation: Part 6 in the diagram represents the vascular cambium, the actively dividing meristematic tissue that lies between the xylem and phloem and continually produces new secondary xylem and phloem cells (parts 5 and 7), driving the plant's secondary growth in girth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The main function of 4 is to
questions.explanation: Part 4 in the diagram represents an outer protective tissue layer (such as the cortex or endodermis) whose main role is to surround and protect the more internal vascular tissues of the stem.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a dicot leaf, guard cells differ from other epidermal cells because they
questions.explanation: Unlike ordinary epidermal cells, guard cells are unique in containing chloroplasts, which allow them to photosynthesize and produce sugars that drive the osmotic changes responsible for opening and closing the stomatal pore.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Herbs differ from shrubs because they
questions.explanation: Herbs have soft, green, non-woody stems and generally stay short, whereas shrubs develop woody stems that branch close to the ground. (Herbs can still be annual or perennial, and both herbs and shrubs may produce fruit, so "does not become woody" is the specific defining distinction.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of monocot plants?
questions.explanation: True secondary thickening (growth in girth via a vascular cambium ring) is a feature of dicots (and gymnosperms), not typical monocots, which generally lack a continuous vascular cambium. Parallel leaf venation, scattered vascular bundles, floral parts in threes, and an often reduced/insignificant perianth are all genuinely characteristic of monocots.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT true of the piliferous layer of a root? It

options.B: is the outermost layer of the cortex
options.D: breaks down as the root ages
options.E: is replaced by cork in old roots

questions.explanation: The piliferous layer is actually the outermost layer of the epidermis of the root (where root hairs originate), not part of the cortex, which lies beneath the epidermis. It does have a thin cuticle (to allow water absorption while offering minimal protection), breaks down as the root matures, and is eventually replaced by protective cork tissue in older roots.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is seed bearing?
questions.explanation: The "whistling pine" (a common name for a conifer such as Casuarina or Araucaria) is a gymnosperm and therefore produces true seeds. Mosses, liverworts, and ferns are all seedless plants that reproduce by spores, and algal filaments do not produce seeds either.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In an angiosperm leaf, the xylem is

options.E: in separate bundles from the phloem

questions.explanation: In the vascular bundles of a typical angiosperm leaf, the xylem is positioned on the upper side of the vein, with the phloem lying below it — so the xylem sits "above" the phloem within each vascular bundle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is common to a dicotyledonous stem and a monocotyledonous root?
questions.explanation: Both a typical dicot stem and a typical monocot root are built around a distinct, wide central pith of parenchyma tissue, with vascular tissue arranged around this pith — a feature they share despite otherwise differing internal arrangements.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following pairs are fully adapted to terrestrial life?
questions.explanation: Flowering plants (angiosperms) and conifers (gymnosperms) both reproduce via pollen and seeds, entirely independent of external water for fertilization, making them fully adapted to a dry, terrestrial existence. Ferns, mosses, and algae, by contrast, all still require a film of water for their motile gametes to achieve fertilization, tying them to moist habitats.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following has cones?
questions.explanation: Gymnosperms (such as conifers) are specifically characterized by bearing their naked seeds in cones, unlike angiosperms (which enclose seeds in fruit), pteridophytes (spore-bearing), or bryophytes (spore-bearing).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The stem differs from the root in having the xylem and phloem strands
questions.explanation: In a typical dicot stem, the xylem and phloem are arranged together in the same vascular bundle, lying along the same radius (with phloem to the outside and xylem to the inside). In the root, by contrast, the xylem and phloem alternate around the central core rather than sitting on the same radius.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The correct sequence of tissues in the anatomy of a young dicotyledonous stem, from the inside to the outside, is

options.A: pith, phloem, cambium, xylem, parenchyma, collenchyma and epidermis
options.B: xylem, phloem, cambium, cortex, endodermis, collenchyma and epidermis
options.C: pith, xylem, cambium, phloem, collenchyma, parenchyma and epidermis
options.D: phloem, xylem, cambium, cortex, endodermis, collenchyma and epidermis

questions.explanation: From the very centre outward, a young dicot stem is arranged as: pith → xylem → cambium → phloem → (cortex, including collenchyma and parenchyma) → epidermis, which matches option C.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Secondary thickening is initiated in a dicotyledonous stem by the
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium is the meristematic (actively dividing) tissue responsible for producing new secondary xylem and secondary phloem, driving the increase in stem girth known as secondary thickening.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements gives the BEST description of bark?

options.B: Cork-like tissues found only in stems
options.C: Brown tissues never found in primary growth

questions.explanation: "Bark" broadly refers to all the tissues lying outside the vascular cambium in a woody stem (including secondary phloem, cork cambium, and cork) — this is the most technically accurate, general description among the options.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the transverse section of the leaf of maize, vascular bundles are arranged in
questions.explanation: In a maize (monocot) leaf cross-section, the vascular bundles are typically arranged in two rows/circles (one closer to the upper surface, one closer to the lower), rather than the single ring seen in many dicot stems.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Double fertilization is a unique feature of
questions.explanation: Double fertilization — where one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg to form the embryo, and a second sperm nucleus fuses with the polar nuclei to form the nutritive endosperm — is a defining reproductive feature unique to flowering plants (angiosperms).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which part of the twig produces auxins?
questions.explanation: Part 1 in the diagram represents the terminal (apical) bud, which is the primary site of auxin (plant growth hormone) production, driving the plant's apical growth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Angiosperms and gymnosperms belong to the plant group known as
questions.explanation: Spermatophyta ("seed plants") is the overarching group that contains both the flowering plants (angiosperms) and the cone-bearing plants (gymnosperms), since both produce true seeds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: To facilitate gaseous exchange, breathing roots have
questions.explanation: Breathing roots (pneumatophores), such as those found in mangrove plants growing in waterlogged, low-oxygen soil, are studded with lenticels — small pores in their surface tissue — that allow atmospheric oxygen to diffuse in for the root's respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A wide pith with a ring of conducting tissue is characteristic of the root of
questions.explanation: A wide central pith surrounded by a ring of vascular tissue is a typical feature of a monocot root, and maize is the classic monocot example among the options given (sunflower, bean, and okra are all dicots, whose roots instead have a small or absent pith with a star-shaped xylem core at the very centre).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The flow of air and water in or out of the mesophyll layer of a leaf is controlled by the
questions.explanation: While the stoma is the actual pore, it is the pair of guard cells flanking it that physically control whether that pore is open or closed, thereby regulating the movement of gases and water vapour in and out of the leaf's internal air spaces.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The major site of photosynthesis in the leaf is the
questions.explanation: The palisade parenchyma (palisade mesophyll) consists of tightly packed, elongated cells directly beneath the upper epidermis, densely loaded with chloroplasts and positioned to receive maximum sunlight — making it the leaf's primary photosynthetic tissue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Production of naked seeds is a distinctive feature of the group of plants called
questions.explanation: Conifers are gymnosperms, meaning their seeds are "naked" — not enclosed within a fruit or ovary wall, but exposed on the surface of cone scales — unlike grasses, legumes, and palms, which are all angiosperms whose seeds develop inside an enclosed fruit.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Secondary thickening in a dicotyledonous stem is controlled by the
questions.explanation: As with the earlier related question, the vascular cambium is the specific meristematic tissue responsible for driving secondary thickening by continuously producing new xylem and phloem cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Stomata pores open when there is

options.A: an increase in the sugar content of guard cells
options.B: a decrease in the osmotic concentration of guard cells
options.C: a decrease in the sugar content of mesophyll cells
options.D: an increase in the sugar content of mesophyll cells

questions.explanation: In the presence of light, guard cells convert stored starch into sugar, which increases their internal solute (osmotic) concentration. Water then moves into the guard cells by osmosis, making them turgid and bowing outward, which opens the stomatal pore.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following structures is capable of producing more tissues in the stem of a herbaceous flowering plant?
questions.explanation: The cambium is a meristematic tissue consisting of actively dividing cells capable of continuously generating new vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), unlike epidermis, mature xylem, or pericycle, which do not routinely produce new tissue in this way.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following features are all associated with monocots?

options.A: Fibrous root system, branched network of veins, and one seed leaf
options.B: Fibrous root system, two seed leaves, and floral parts in threes
options.C: One seed leaf, petals in threes or groups of threes, and parallel venation of leaves
options.D: One seed leaf, net-veined leaves, and petals in three or multiples of three

questions.explanation: A single seed leaf (cotyledon), floral parts in threes, and parallel leaf venation are all classic, consistent monocot features occurring together, whereas the other options mix in dicot traits (branched/net venation or two seed leaves) that don't belong with true monocot anatomy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Peripheral arrangement of vascular tissues in dicots is a characteristic of the
questions.explanation: In a dicot stem, the vascular bundles are typically arranged in a ring toward the periphery (outer region) around a central pith — a very different pattern from the central, star-shaped xylem core found in a dicot root.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Most monocots are easily recognized by their
questions.explanation: Most monocot plants (such as grasses) have characteristically long, narrow, sword-shaped leaves with parallel veins and typically no distinct petiole, making this a useful field identification feature.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the internal structure of plants, a wide pith in the centre is common to
questions.explanation: Both a typical dicot stem and a typical monocot root feature a distinct, wide central pith surrounded by vascular tissue — this shared internal layout is what connects these two specific structures (a dicot root, by contrast, generally lacks a large central pith, having a star-shaped xylem core instead).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Angiosperms and gymnosperms belong to the class known as
questions.explanation: As established earlier, both angiosperms and gymnosperms are seed plants and are together classified under Spermatophyta.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The part of the plant where photosynthesis is least likely to take place is
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, part IV corresponds to a non-green, underground, or woody part of the plant (such as the root or a bud lacking chlorophyll), which receives little or no light and therefore carries out little to no photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the transverse section of a dicot stem, the region lying between the endodermis and the vascular bundle is the
questions.explanation: The pericycle is the thin layer of tissue lying just inside the endodermis, directly surrounding the vascular bundles in a dicot stem, and it is also the tissue from which lateral roots later originate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Monocot stems differ from dicot stems in that monocots have
questions.explanation: Monocot stems generally lack a continuous vascular cambium ring, which is why they typically do not undergo true secondary thickening the way dicot stems do — instead, their numerous vascular bundles are scattered throughout the stem rather than arranged in an organized cambium-bearing ring.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The opening and closing of the stoma are regulated by
questions.explanation: As explained earlier, the turgor changes in guard cells that open and close the stomatal pore are driven by osmosis — water moving into or out of the guard cells in response to changing internal sugar/solute concentrations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a dicotyledonous stem, the zone between the epidermis and the pericycle is the
questions.explanation: The cortex is the region of ground tissue lying between the outer epidermis and the inner pericycle/vascular tissue (stele) of a dicot stem, with its innermost layer specifically called the endodermis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is true of the transverse section of a dicot stem?

options.A: The xylem is more interiorly located than the phloem
options.B: The cambium lies between the cortex and vascular bundles
options.C: The vascular bundles are randomly scattered within the cortex
options.D: The epidermis is completely encircled by the cortex

questions.explanation: In each vascular bundle of a dicot stem, the xylem is positioned toward the inside (nearer the pith), with the phloem lying further out (toward the cortex) — making the xylem the more interiorly located tissue. Dicot vascular bundles are arranged in an organized ring, not randomly scattered, and it is the epidermis that surrounds the cortex, not the reverse.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Seed plants are divided into
questions.explanation: At the broadest level, seed plants (Spermatophyta) are divided into the two major groups angiosperms (flowering plants, with enclosed seeds) and gymnosperms (cone-bearing plants, with naked seeds). Monocots and dicots is a further subdivision specifically within angiosperms, not of seed plants as a whole.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Plants that show secondary growth are usually found among the
questions.explanation: True secondary growth (increase in girth via a functional vascular cambium) is characteristic of dicotyledonous plants (and gymnosperms), while thallophytes, pteridophytes, and most monocots typically do not show this kind of woody secondary thickening.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following plant structures lacks a waterproof cuticle?
questions.explanation: Unlike the leaf, stem, and general shoot system (all of which are covered by a waterproof cuticle to prevent excess water loss), the root's absorbing surface (epidermis/root hairs) lacks this cuticle, since a cuticle would block the very water absorption the root needs to perform.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is involved in secondary thickening in plants?
questions.explanation: Secondary thickening in woody dicot stems is driven jointly by two lateral meristems: the vascular cambium, which produces new wood (secondary xylem) and increases the stem's girth internally, and the cork cambium, which produces the protective bark (cork) on the outside.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Seed plants are the most dominant vegetation on land because of
questions.explanation: Seed plants owe much of their dominance on land to their efficient means of seed dispersal (by wind, animals, water, and other mechanisms), allowing them to colonize new areas widely and successfully — unlike more primitive plants, which remain tied to water for reproduction due to their motile gametes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which one of these animals is NEVER a secondary host of tapeworms?
questions.explanation: In the tapeworm (Taenia) life cycle, man is always the primary (definitive) host — the one in which the adult tapeworm lives and reproduces in the intestine — never a secondary (intermediate) host. Cattle and pigs, by contrast, commonly serve as secondary hosts, harboring the larval bladderworm stage in their muscles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The two types of human tapeworm can be distinguished by the presence or absence of
questions.explanation: Taenia solium (the pork tapeworm) has a scolex armed with hooks as well as suckers, whereas Taenia saginata (the beef tapeworm) has a scolex with suckers only and no hooks. This presence or absence of hooks is the key distinguishing feature between the two species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A tapeworm has no alimentary canal because

options.E: the suckers on the scolex suck blood

questions.explanation: A tapeworm lives permanently within the host's small intestine, bathed in food that the host has already fully digested. It simply absorbs these ready-made nutrients directly across its body surface, so it has no need for its own digestive/alimentary canal at all.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Flatworms and roundworms are said to be invertebrates because
questions.explanation: "Invertebrate" specifically means lacking a backbone (vertebral column) — flatworms (platyhelminthes) and roundworms (nematodes) fit this definition regardless of their size, parasitic lifestyle, or where they live.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of these worms is beneficial to man?
questions.explanation: The earthworm is beneficial because it aerates and improves soil structure, adds humus by breaking down organic matter, and improves overall soil fertility and texture. The other worms listed (hookworm, tapeworm, roundworm, guinea worm) are all human/animal parasites that cause disease.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Exoskeleton is NOT found in the
questions.explanation: The earthworm belongs to the annelids, which have soft, segmented bodies without any hard external skeleton — instead they rely on a fluid-filled hydrostatic skeleton for support. Maggots, mosquito larvae, caterpillars, and termites are all insect (arthropod) forms that possess a chitinous exoskeleton, even at their larval stages.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The parts used by tapeworm to fasten itself to the host's intestine are the
questions.explanation: The scolex (head) of the tapeworm is armed with all three attachment structures together — a rostellum (a small protruding structure), hooks, and suckers — which combine to grip firmly onto the wall of the host's intestine.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of these animals is radially symmetrical?
questions.explanation: Hydra, a coelenterate, has a body plan organized around a central axis, so it can be divided into two identical halves along any longitudinal plane passing through that axis — this is radial symmetry. Squid, snail, and cockroach are all bilaterally symmetrical, with only one plane of symmetry (dividing left from right).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following lacks chaetae, tentacles and antennae?
questions.explanation: A snail possesses tentacles (for sensing) but lacks the bristle-like chaetae (found in earthworms) and the antennae (found in arthropods like crabs and millipedes) — so overall it is the odd one out lacking chaetae AND antennae among these structures.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A good example of a diploblastic organism is
questions.explanation: Hydra (a coelenterate) is built from just two cell/tissue layers — an outer ectoderm and inner endoderm — making it diploblastic. Amoeba is unicellular (not applicable), while earthworms and roundworms are triploblastic, having a third middle layer, the mesoderm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The function of the clitellum in the earthworm is to
questions.explanation: The clitellum is the visibly swollen, glandular band found on an earthworm's body, and its specific function is to secrete the mucus-based cocoon in which the fertilized eggs are stored and protected during development.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In tapeworm, the two structures that run through the length of the body are the

options.A: nerve cord and the excretory duct
options.B: sperm duct and the nerve cord
options.C: genital pore and the excretory duct
options.D: sperm duct and the genital pore

questions.explanation: A tapeworm has a longitudinal nerve cord and paired excretory (osmoregulatory) ducts that both run the entire length of its ribbon-like body, joined by a cross-connecting tube near the posterior end of each segment (proglottis).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of snails?

options.D: Soft unsegmented body in a mantle

questions.explanation: Snails secrete a hard calcareous (calcium carbonate) shell, not a chitinous exoskeleton (which is a feature of arthropods like insects). Snails do show bilateral symmetry, move using a muscular foot, and have a soft, unsegmented body enclosed by a mantle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The following organisms are hermaphrodites EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Unlike snails, tapeworms, and earthworms, which are all hermaphroditic (each individual possesses both male and female reproductive organs), Schistosoma (the blood fluke) is unusual among flatworms in having separate sexes — distinct male and female individuals.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Parasitic forms are NOT found among
questions.explanation: Molluscs (like snails, clams, octopuses) are essentially all free-living, with no significant parasitic representatives — unlike platyhelminthes (e.g. tapeworms, flukes), nematodes (e.g. hookworms, roundworms), and even annelids (e.g. leeches), all of which include well-known parasitic members.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following sets of organisms represents the correct trend from simple to complex structural organization? (1) Mollusca (2) Platyhelminthes (3) Nematoda (4) Protozoa
questions.explanation: Structural complexity increases from single-celled Protozoa (4, simplest) to the simple flatworm body plan of Platyhelminthes (2), then to the slightly more complex tube-within-a-tube body plan of Nematoda (3), and finally to the more elaborately organized body of Mollusca (1, most complex among these) — giving the order 4, 2, 3, 1.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At which stage in this cycle can man be infected?
questions.explanation: Based on the tapeworm life cycle in the diagram, man becomes infected at the stage where the bladderworm (cysticercus) larva, present in undercooked pork or beef, is eaten — this corresponds to stage 4 in the numbered cycle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which stage is found in the muscle of an infected pig?
questions.explanation: Stage 4 in the diagram also represents the bladderworm (cysticercus) larval stage that develops and lodges within the muscle tissue of the intermediate host (pig or cattle), which is precisely where it is later ingested by man in improperly cooked meat.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A characteristic of the phylum coelenterate is that

options.B: they possess a gut with a single opening
options.C: they possess numerous pores on their body

questions.explanation: Coelenterates (e.g. Hydra, jellyfish, coral) have a simple body plan with a single gut opening (called the enteron) that serves as both mouth and anus, unlike more advanced animals with a separate mouth and anus. (Numerous body pores is a feature of sponges, not coelenterates, and coelenterates are radially, not bilaterally, symmetrical.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following phyla have members with both internal and external segmentation?
questions.explanation: In tapeworms (Platyhelminthes), the external segmentation of the body into proglottides is matched by corresponding internal segmentation (each proglottis containing its own reproductive organs), representing both internal and external division — a feature not shared in the same way by nematodes, algae, or molluscs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The body of a snail is divided into
questions.explanation: A snail's body is fundamentally organized into two main parts: the visceral mass (containing the internal organs, housed within the coiled shell) and the muscular foot (used for locomotion) — a body plan quite different from the head-thorax-abdomen arrangement seen in insects.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Hydra removes undigested food by

options.D: egesting it through the body surface

questions.explanation: Since Hydra has only a single opening (the mouth, which also serves as the "enteron" opening) leading into its gut cavity, undigested food waste must be expelled back out through this same mouth opening, as there is no separate anus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following groups of invertebrates reproduces by budding?
questions.explanation: Coelenterates such as Hydra commonly reproduce asexually by budding — a small outgrowth forms on the body wall, develops into a miniature version of the parent, and eventually detaches to live independently — a method not typical of arthropods, annelids, or molluscs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the tapeworm, the suckers on the scolex are used for

options.A: sucking the blood of the host

questions.explanation: The suckers on a tapeworm's scolex (head) function purely as attachment organs, gripping firmly onto the wall of the host's intestine to prevent the worm from being swept away by the flow of digested food — tapeworms do not feed on blood at all, since they absorb pre-digested nutrients through their body surface.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Sting cells are normally found in
questions.explanation: Stinging cells (cnidoblasts, containing nematocysts) are a defining feature of coelenterates such as Hydra, used for both capturing prey and for defence — they are not found in flatworms, snails, or Paramecium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the earthworm, the cocoon is secreted by the
questions.explanation: As noted earlier, the clitellum (the visibly swollen glandular band on the earthworm's body) is specifically responsible for secreting the mucus cocoon used to protect the fertilized eggs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The respiratory organ in the land snail is the
questions.explanation: In land snails, the mantle (specifically a well-vascularized region of it, forming a simple "lung") is the organ responsible for gaseous exchange with the air. The radula is a feeding structure, and the tentacles and foot are sensory/locomotory structures, unrelated to respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A major difference between platyhelminthes and coelenterates is that platyhelminthes
questions.explanation: Platyhelminthes (flatworms) are triploblastic, possessing a third middle tissue layer, the mesoderm, in addition to ectoderm and endoderm — unlike coelenterates, which remain diploblastic (only ectoderm and endoderm). Both groups are multicellular, and both can reproduce sexually or asexually depending on species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The essential structural difference between Hydra and tapeworm is that while Hydra

options.C: has a mouth, tapeworm feeds by suckers

questions.explanation: This distinction directly parallels the previous question: Hydra is a coelenterate with only two tissue layers (diploblastic), while the tapeworm, a flatworm, has three tissue layers including a mesoderm (triploblastic) — this is the fundamental structural difference between them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The soil swallowed by the earthworm to form the worm cast is ground up in the
questions.explanation: As the earthworm swallows soil (along with organic matter) while burrowing, this material passes into the muscular gizzard, where it is ground up against small stones the worm has also ingested, before being expelled as the familiar worm cast.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The cnidoblast cells found in Hydra are used for
questions.explanation: Cnidoblasts (nematoblasts) are specialized stinging cells that fire out thread-like, sometimes venomous structures used both to capture prey (offence) and to fend off potential predators (defence).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Annelids differ from nematodes in that they
questions.explanation: Annelids (like earthworms) are distinguished by true metameric segmentation — their bodies are divided into a series of repeating, similar segments, each often with its own set of internal structures — a feature nematodes (roundworms) lack, even though both groups are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, and have complete digestive systems.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In snails, the hard calcareous shells are secreted by the
questions.explanation: The mantle, a specialized layer of tissue that covers the snail's visceral mass, is responsible for secreting the layers of calcium carbonate that build up the snail's hard external shell.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The habitat of the Cysticercus of Taenia solium is
questions.explanation: Taenia solium is specifically the pork tapeworm, so its larval bladderworm (Cysticercus) stage develops and resides in the muscle tissue of the pig, its intermediate host — not in cattle, which are instead the intermediate host for the beef tapeworm, Taenia saginata.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The division of a body into two equal halves along a longitudinal plane is called
questions.explanation: When an animal's body can only be divided into two identical (mirror-image) halves along one specific plane running from front to back, this is the definition of bilateral symmetry.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Coelom is absent in the class of animals termed
questions.explanation: Coelenterates are diploblastic, with no mesoderm layer at all, so they cannot have a true coelom (a mesoderm-lined body cavity) — molluscs, reptiles, and arthropods, all being more complex triploblastic animals, do possess (or evolved from ancestors with) a coelom.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An example of a radially symmetrical organism is
questions.explanation: As established earlier, Hydra's body is organized around a central axis, allowing it to be divided into identical halves along any of several longitudinal planes — the defining feature of radial symmetry. Planaria, tapeworm, and roundworm are all bilaterally symmetrical.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The leech and the earthworm belong to the
questions.explanation: Both leeches and earthworms are segmented worms belonging to the phylum Annelida, sharing features such as a soft, ringed (segmented) body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: One primitive feature of the coelenterates is the possession of
questions.explanation: Radial symmetry (a body organized around a central axis rather than a left-right mirror plan) is considered an evolutionarily simpler, more primitive body arrangement, characteristic of the coelenterates, compared to the more advanced bilateral symmetry seen in higher animal groups.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the organisms is characterized by the possession of a chitinous exoskeleton?
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, organism I is depicted as an insect (or other arthropod), and arthropods are specifically defined by having a hard, chitinous exoskeleton covering their jointed bodies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The type of reproduction illustrated in IV is
questions.explanation: Organism IV in the diagram is shown reproducing by budding — a small outgrowth developing on the parent's body and eventually detaching as a new individual — a classic asexual reproductive method used by coelenterates such as Hydra.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Radial symmetry is a feature common to the
questions.explanation: As established throughout this topic, radial symmetry is the hallmark body plan of the coelenterates, distinguishing them from the bilaterally symmetrical platyhelminthes, nematodes, and arthropods.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The habitat of the organism is

options.C: under leaf litter on forest floor
options.D: the small intestine of large vertebrates

questions.explanation: Based on the diagram (an earthworm-type or aquatic annelid organism), its natural habitat corresponds to moist environments such as slow-moving streams and marshes, rather than being an internal parasite of a host animal (which would apply to worms like tapeworms).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is most advanced in the evolutionary trend of animals?
questions.explanation: The cockroach is an arthropod, representing the most structurally advanced and complex body organization among these four options — having jointed appendages, a well-developed nervous system, and specialized body regions — placing it ahead of the snail (mollusc), earthworm (annelid), and liver fluke (flatworm) on the evolutionary complexity scale.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An animal body that can be cut along its axis in any plane to give two identical parts is said to be
questions.explanation: This is precisely the definition of radial symmetry — the body can be divided into matching halves through multiple different planes passing through its central axis, unlike bilateral symmetry, where only one specific plane produces mirror-image halves.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Taenia solium can be found in
questions.explanation: As established earlier, Taenia solium is the pork tapeworm, using the pig as its intermediate host, in whose muscle tissue the larval bladderworm stage develops.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The organism is found in soils rich in
questions.explanation: Earthworms thrive in soils rich in humus (decomposed organic matter), which provides both the moisture and the organic food material they need to survive and feed on as they burrow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The young proglottides of the organism are represented by
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, part IV corresponds to the neck region of the tapeworm, which is the area of active growth where new, young proglottides (body segments) are continuously produced, with older, more mature proglottides pushed further toward the tail end of the worm as new ones form.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of these is not true of the insect? The possession of
questions.explanation: An insect has only one pair of antennae, not two. Jointed appendages, an exoskeleton, three pairs of legs, and a segmented body are all genuine, defining features of insects.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Insects show considerable powers of water conservation. This is due to the fact that

options.A: the chitinous cuticle is impregnated with tanned proteins
options.B: nitrogenous waste is eliminated as urea
options.D: the Malpighian tubules are impermeable to water
options.E: the cuticle is covered with wax

questions.explanation: The insect's outer chitinous cuticle is coated with a thin waxy layer, which is highly effective at preventing water loss through the body surface — this waxy coating is the specific adaptation responsible for insects' impressive water conservation, more so than the chitin itself or any other listed feature.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A mosquito which produces eggs with a float, and whose larvae lie horizontal to the water surface, and which also rests at an angle on a vertical surface, is
questions.explanation: These are all classic identifying features of the Anopheles mosquito (the malaria vector): its eggs have floats and are laid singly, its larvae rest horizontally/parallel just under the water surface, and the resting adult characteristically tilts its body at an angle to the surface it perches on — unlike Culex or Aedes mosquitoes, which show different egg, larval, and resting postures.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following insects has an incomplete metamorphosis during its life cycle?
questions.explanation: The grasshopper develops through incomplete (hemimetabolous) metamorphosis — egg → nymph → adult — where the nymph closely resembles a smaller, wingless version of the adult. Butterflies, bees, mosquitoes, and houseflies all undergo complete metamorphosis instead, passing through a distinct larval and pupal stage that looks nothing like the adult.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of these statements is NOT true of insects? They

options.B: have a body divided into three distinct regions of head, thorax and abdomen
options.C: have a thorax comprising three segments, only two of which bear a pair of appendages each

questions.explanation: In fact, all three segments of an insect's thorax (prothorax, mesothorax, and metathorax) each bear one pair of walking legs — making the claim that "only two" segments bear appendages the false statement here. Insects genuinely are arthropods, have a head-thorax-abdomen body plan, breathe through a network of tracheae, and (in most cases) undergo metamorphosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A centipede differs from a millipede by its

options.C: paired legs on each abdominal segment

questions.explanation: Centipedes possess a pair of venomous poison claws (modified first legs, called forcipules) just behind the head, used to inject venom into prey — a feature millipedes entirely lack. (Millipedes, in contrast, tend to have a more cylindrical body and two pairs of legs per body segment, rather than one.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: 'Jointed skeleton' is absent in the
questions.explanation: The snail is a mollusc, not an arthropod, and so it lacks a jointed external skeleton entirely (having instead a soft body sometimes protected by a coiled calcareous shell). Cockroaches, spiders, millipedes, and dragonflies are all arthropods with a jointed chitinous exoskeleton.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following invertebrates does NOT possess antennae?
questions.explanation: Spiders belong to the arachnids, which lack antennae altogether; instead, they use a pair of pedipalpi (grasping/sensory appendages) near the mouth. Centipedes, crustaceans, millipedes, and insects all possess antennae.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Each of the following is an arthropod EXCEPT the
questions.explanation: As established in an earlier question, the snail is a mollusc, not an arthropod — crabs, spiders, millipedes, and cockroaches are all true arthropods.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Incomplete metamorphosis occurs in the
questions.explanation: As noted earlier, the grasshopper undergoes incomplete (hemimetabolous) metamorphosis, while the butterfly, mosquito, and housefly all undergo complete metamorphosis with a distinct larval and pupal stage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: When the original king and queen of termites die, they are replaced by

options.A: the king and queen of another colony
options.B: some adult reproductives from the same colony
options.C: some adult workers which are specially fed to breed
options.D: developing nymphs nurtured as secondary reproductives

questions.explanation: A termite colony maintains its egg-laying rate by rearing several developing nymphs into secondary (replacement) reproductives, which can then take over the roles of a deceased king or queen — the colony does not simply promote ordinary workers or import royalty from another colony.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The male cockroach differs from the female by having
questions.explanation: A pair of small style-like structures near the tip of the abdomen is a feature unique to the male cockroach. A pair of cerci, mandibles, and spiracles are present in both sexes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The crayfish is an arthropod because

options.A: its body consists of a cephalothorax and an abdomen
options.B: it has a pair each of antennae and antennules
options.C: every segment of its body carries a pair of appendages
options.D: its body is covered with an exoskeleton made of chitin

questions.explanation: The defining feature that places the crayfish (and all arthropods) into the phylum Arthropoda is the possession of a hard, jointed, chitinous exoskeleton — the other features listed (body regions, antennae, appendages per segment) are true of crayfish but are not, by themselves, the defining criterion for arthropod classification.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the life history of a butterfly, destruction of crops is caused by the
questions.explanation: The caterpillar (larval stage of a butterfly) is the voracious, leaf-eating stage responsible for damaging crops, whereas the adult butterfly is actually beneficial, acting as a pollinator.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Insects and millipede have many features in common EXCEPT
questions.explanation: While insects possess a pair of true compound eyes, millipedes may have simple eyes, compound eyes, or none at all, depending on the species — making compound eyes not a consistently shared feature. Both groups do have a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, and segmented bodies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a common characteristic of crustaceans?

options.A: Possession of a pair of antennae
options.B: Possession of two pairs of antennae
options.C: Each segment has a pair of walking legs
options.D: Four pairs of walking legs on the cephalothorax

questions.explanation: A defining feature of crustaceans (such as crayfish and crabs) is that they possess two pairs of antennae (antennae and antennules), unlike insects, which have only one pair.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The pedipalpi in spiders are used for
questions.explanation: Spiders primarily use their pedipalpi to grasp and manipulate captured prey, though they also serve a secondary sensory role (being sensitive to touch). They are not used for walking (spiders have separate walking legs) or for spinning silk (which is done by spinnerets).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The function of maxillipeds in crayfish is to aid
questions.explanation: The maxillipeds in a crayfish are specialized appendages positioned near the mouth that help manipulate, chop, and pass food into the mouth, assisting in feeding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following insects undergoes incomplete metamorphosis?
questions.explanation: Termites, like grasshoppers, develop through incomplete metamorphosis (egg → nymph → adult), while mosquitoes, houseflies, and moths all undergo complete metamorphosis with distinct larval and pupal stages.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The butterfly is of great economic importance because

options.A: of its use in scientific studies
options.C: it adds to the beauty of the environment
options.D: it pollinates flowers of crops and other plants

questions.explanation: While butterflies do feed on nectar and are admired for their beauty, their most significant economic importance lies in pollination — as they visit flowers for nectar, they transfer pollen between plants, directly benefiting the reproduction of crops and other flowering plants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The mouth part of the insect is adapted for
questions.explanation: The cockroach has strong mandibles adapted for biting and chewing solid food, unlike insects such as the mosquito (piercing and sucking) or housefly (sponging/lapping), which have very differently adapted mouthparts for liquid feeding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following insects lays its eggs in horny, purse-like cases?
questions.explanation: The cockroach lays its eggs enclosed within a hardened, purse-shaped protective case called an ootheca, which shields the developing eggs until they hatch.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The group of insects that undergoes complete metamorphosis is
questions.explanation: Houseflies, beetles, and butterflies all undergo complete metamorphosis, passing through egg, larva, pupa, and adult stages. Cockroaches, grasshoppers, and aphids, by contrast, develop through incomplete metamorphosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The three classes in a termitarium are
questions.explanation: A termite colony's caste system is organized into three broad functional classes: workers (who feed and maintain the colony), soldiers (who defend it), and reproductives (including the king, queen, and any secondary reproductives responsible for producing offspring).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The ability of the cockroach to live in cracks and crevices is enhanced by the possession of
questions.explanation: The cockroach's characteristically flattened (dorso-ventrally compressed) body shape allows it to squeeze into narrow cracks and crevices for shelter and protection, a key adaptation for its lifestyle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The caste of termites that lacks pigmentation is the
questions.explanation: Worker termites are typically pale, whitish, and unpigmented, since they spend their entire lives inside the dark termite mound/nest and have no need for protective pigmentation — this pale appearance is also why termites are commonly (though incorrectly) nicknamed "white ants."

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the honey bee colony, the drones are

options.A: sterile males with reduced mouth parts
options.B: sterile males with well-developed mouth parts
options.C: fertile males with reduced mouth parts
options.D: fertile males with well-developed mouth parts

questions.explanation: Drones are the fertile male bees of the colony, whose sole role is to mate with the queen; their mouthparts are comparatively reduced since they are fed by the workers rather than needing to forage for themselves.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The group of Arthropods that has no antennae is the
questions.explanation: As noted earlier, arachnids (spiders, scorpions, mites, ticks) are the arthropod group that lacks antennae entirely, using pedipalpi instead for sensory and grasping functions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The jointed structure in insects that bears organs which are sensitive to touch, smell and vibration is the
questions.explanation: The antenna is the jointed sensory appendage responsible for detecting touch, smell, and vibration in insects, distinguishing it from the maxilla and labium (both feeding-related mouthparts) and the abdomen (the rear body region).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Water fleas, wood lice and barnacles belong to the group
questions.explanation: Water fleas, wood lice, and barnacles are all classified within the Crustacea, a diverse arthropod group typically characterized by two pairs of antennae and (often) an aquatic lifestyle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The role of the male adult honey bee is to
questions.explanation: The sole functional role of the male honey bee (drone) is reproductive — to mate with the queen. Cleaning the hive, ventilating it, and caring for the young are all duties carried out by the sterile female worker bees.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: When oil is poured into the breeding site of mosquitoes, it
questions.explanation: A film of oil poured over standing water spreads across the surface and blocks the mosquito larvae's access to atmospheric air (which they breathe through a surface-piercing siphon), effectively suffocating them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A feature of the caste systems of bees and termites is that

options.B: the kings are bigger than queens
options.D: nuptial flight is performed by all members

questions.explanation: In both bee and termite colonies, the worker caste consists of sterile individuals who forgo reproduction to instead perform maintenance, foraging, and caregiving tasks for the colony — reproduction is reserved for the queen (and king, in termites) and any reproductive castes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Insects are considered the most successful among Invertebrates because they

options.D: possess the ability to change their forms

questions.explanation: Insects are considered the single most successful animal group largely because of their remarkable adaptability — they are found thriving in an enormous range of habitats and environmental conditions worldwide, far more so than would be explained by any one single feature like wings, exoskeletons, or metamorphosis alone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The larval stage of a mosquito is called
questions.explanation: The aquatic, actively wriggling larval stage of a mosquito is commonly called a "wriggler," distinct from the terms used for other insect larvae (maggot for flies, grub for beetles, caterpillar for butterflies/moths).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The function of the long-winged reproductives in a termite colony is to
questions.explanation: The long-winged reproductive termites exist specifically to fly off from the colony in large numbers (swarming) in order to disperse and establish entirely new colonies elsewhere, preventing overcrowding in the original nest.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The stage in the life history of a moth responsible for the destruction of agricultural crops is the
questions.explanation: As with the butterfly, it is the caterpillar (larval) stage of the moth that feeds voraciously on plant leaves and is responsible for crop damage, while the adult moth (imago) generally does far less feeding-related damage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The only caste in the termite colony whose members can feed themselves is the
questions.explanation: Worker termites are the only caste capable of independently feeding themselves (and are also uniquely able to digest cellulose); they are then responsible for feeding all the other castes, including the reproductives, soldiers, and developing young, who cannot feed themselves.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The process of shedding the exoskeleton of an arthropod is known as
questions.explanation: The periodic shedding (moulting) of the rigid exoskeleton to allow for growth is specifically termed ecdysis; the developmental stage between two successive moults is called an instar.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is common to the mosquito, housefly and blackfly?

options.D: Their adults have two pairs of wings

questions.explanation: The mosquito, housefly, and blackfly are all true flies (Diptera) that undergo complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult). (Not all of them are aquatic at every immature stage, none are true "parasites" of man in the strict sense, and flies characteristically have only one pair of functional wings, not two.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The most abundant group of organisms in the animal kingdom is
questions.explanation: Insects (class Insecta) make up roughly 70% of all known animal species, vastly outnumbering mammals, birds, and annelids combined, making them by far the most abundant and diverse animal group.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following animals is most adapted for water conservation?
questions.explanation: As discussed earlier, insects possess a waxy, waterproof cuticle that dramatically reduces water loss by evaporation, and they excrete nitrogenous waste as nearly solid uric acid (rather than urine), further conserving water — making them exceptionally well adapted to water conservation compared with earthworms, mammals, or flatworms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The main distinguishing features between the soldier termite and other members of the caste are the

options.A: presence of wings, possession of a large thorax and a small head
options.B: absence of wings, possession of strong mandibles and a large head
options.C: absence of wings, possession of big head and mandible
options.D: presence of wings, possession of a small head and large thorax

questions.explanation: Soldier termites are specifically distinguished by being wingless and having a disproportionately large head equipped with strong, well-developed mandibles (or, in some species, a pointed nasus for chemical defence) — features specialized for defending the colony against invaders.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the organisms represented are notable agricultural pests?
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, organisms I and IV correspond to a grasshopper and a caterpillar (larval moth/butterfly) respectively — both well known as destructive, leaf-eating agricultural pests.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An economic importance of the organism represented by IV is that

options.B: it helps in the control of mosquito larvae
options.C: it transmits water-borne diseases to humans
options.D: it is destructive to farm crops

questions.explanation: As identified above, organism IV (the caterpillar) is economically significant chiefly because of the damage it inflicts on farm crops through its voracious leaf-feeding habit.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The adult form of III is a vector of
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, organism III corresponds to a mosquito, whose adult form is a vector for the filarial worm — the parasite responsible for causing elephantiasis (severe swelling of the limbs due to blocked lymphatic vessels).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The adaptive importance of nuptial flight from termite colonies is to

options.A: ensure cross-breeding between members of one colony and another
options.B: expel the reproductives so as to provide enough food for other members
options.C: disperse the reproductives in order to establish new colonies
options.D: provide abundant food for birds and other animals during the early rains

questions.explanation: Nuptial (mating) flights allow winged reproductive termites to leave the parent colony, pair up with reproductives from other colonies, and disperse to new locations where they can found entirely new, independent colonies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An arthropod that is destructive at the early stage of its life cycle is
questions.explanation: As established earlier, the butterfly's early (larval/caterpillar) stage is the destructive, crop-damaging phase of its life cycle, whereas the adult butterfly is actually beneficial as a pollinator.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The significance of a very large number of termites involved in nuptial swarming is to

options.A: provide birds with plenty of food
options.B: ensure their perpetuation despite predatory pressure
options.C: search for a favourable place to breed
options.D: ensure that every individual gets a mate

questions.explanation: Because so many termites (and their predators, such as birds) are active during a nuptial swarm, huge numbers of the winged reproductives are lost to predation — but by swarming in such vast numbers, enough individuals still survive to found new colonies, ensuring the species' continued survival despite this heavy predation pressure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following describes a characteristic of arthropods?

options.A: The organism has a pair of jointed appendages
options.B: The body is not divided into a number of segments
options.C: The body is covered by chitin
options.D: The organism finds it easy to grow freely

questions.explanation: A chitinous exoskeleton covering the body is a universal, defining characteristic of arthropods. (Their bodies are, in fact, segmented, they have many jointed appendages rather than just "a pair," and their rigid exoskeleton actually restricts free growth, requiring periodic moulting instead.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following distinguishes a butterfly from a moth?

options.A: Both are active during the day
options.C: The abdomen of a moth is fatter than that of a butterfly
options.D: The wings of a butterfly rest horizontally but those of a moth rest vertically

questions.explanation: Moths typically have a noticeably fatter, hairier abdomen than the slimmer-bodied butterfly. (Butterflies are generally diurnal while moths are typically nocturnal, their antennae differ in shape — butterflies have knobbed antennae, moths often feathery ones — and it is actually butterflies that rest with wings held vertically, while moths rest with wings spread horizontally, the reverse of option D.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Proboscis is a structure that is mostly found in
questions.explanation: A proboscis — a long, often tubular or coiled mouthpart used for feeding on liquids — is a structure most characteristically associated with insects (such as the coiled proboscis of a butterfly, used for sucking nectar).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The part numbered 12 is
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram in the source text, part 12 corresponds to the opercular plate — the bony flap (operculum), also popularly called the "gill cover," that protects the gills on the side of a bony fish's head.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: During the movement of the fish from point A to target B, one of these parts is not involved
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, part 10 (representing a structure such as a scale, unconnected with active movement) plays no functional role in the fish's locomotion, unlike the fins (parts such as 3, 5, 6, and 7), which actively contribute to propulsion, steering, and balance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The feature that distinguishes the toad or frog from a fish is the absence of
questions.explanation: Adult toads and frogs have soft, moist, scaleless skin, unlike fish, which are covered in protective scales — this is the clearest distinguishing feature among the options (frogs do have lungs as adults, and both groups have paired appendages/limbs in some form).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which of these is not associated with the tadpole stages of the toad or frog?
questions.explanation: Amphibian eggs (and the tadpoles that hatch from them) are surrounded by a soft jelly coating, not a hard shell — a shell is instead characteristic of reptile and bird eggs. The V-shaped cement gland, external gills (later covered by an operculum), and jelly coating are all genuinely part of early tadpole development.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Some of the features of an animal are scales, teeth, nares and backbone. The animal is likely to be a
questions.explanation: A lizard has scaly skin, teeth, nostrils (nares), and a backbone, matching all the given features — toads lack scales, birds lack teeth, and rats/bats (mammals) lack the typical reptilian scaly covering.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which of the following animals is cold-blooded?
questions.explanation: The lizard is a reptile and therefore ectothermic (cold-blooded), meaning its body temperature varies with its surroundings. Cats, whales, birds, and horses are all warm-blooded (endothermic) animals that maintain a constant internal body temperature.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The main function of the swim-bladder is for
questions.explanation: The swim bladder is a gas-filled sac found in bony fishes that allows them to control their buoyancy, adjusting how much they float or sink in the water without expending extra muscular energy. (In some fish, such as lungfish, it can additionally assist with breathing, but its main, universal role is buoyancy control.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: When an operculate fish breathes, it takes in water through the

options.A: mouth and passes it out through the same way
options.B: mouth and passes it out through the operculum
options.C: operculum and passes it out through the mouth
options.D: operculum and passes it out through the nostrils
options.E: nostrils and passes it out through the operculum

questions.explanation: A fish with an operculum (gill cover) draws water in through its mouth, passes it over the gills for gas exchange, and then expels it out from under the operculum — a one-way flow that keeps oxygenated water constantly moving across the gill surfaces.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which of the following structures is NOT found in the female Agama lizard?
questions.explanation: "Pre-natal pads" (nuptial/copulatory pads) are not a feature found in female Agama lizards at all — features like the ear drum, gular fold (throat flap), nasal scale, and nuchal crest are present in the Agama lizard's general anatomy, though some (like a prominent crest or red coloring) tend to be more developed in males.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The male toad differs from the female by having
questions.explanation: Male toads possess vocal sacs, inflatable pouches used to amplify their mating calls — a feature females lack. Vocal sacs are directly tied to the male's role in courtship calling.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The dorsal and anal fins of fish are used for
questions.explanation: The dorsal (top) and anal (underside) fins act like keels, helping to stabilize the fish and prevent it from rolling side to side as it swims, rather than directly controlling upward/downward movement (which is more the role of paired fins) or steering (caudal fin).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: In fish, the sense organs which detect movements in the water are located within the
questions.explanation: The lateral line is a specialized sensory system running along the sides of a fish's body, containing cells sensitive to water vibrations and pressure changes, allowing the fish to detect movement and disturbances in the surrounding water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: At what stage in the life history of a toad is its mode of breathing similar to that of a fish?
questions.explanation: During the internal gill stage of tadpole development, the toad breathes using gills enclosed within an operculum — structurally and functionally very similar to how a true fish breathes, before the tadpole eventually develops lungs as it matures into an adult.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Fishes are cold-blooded because their body temperature is

options.C: dependent on that of their surroundings

questions.explanation: Being cold-blooded (poikilothermic/ectothermic) specifically means an animal's internal body temperature fluctuates with, and is dependent on, the temperature of its external environment — it is not necessarily "constantly low," since a fish's temperature could actually be quite warm if its surrounding water is warm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The fins making up the limbs of the bony fish are
questions.explanation: The paired pectoral and pelvic fins of a bony fish are considered analogous to the fore and hind limbs of other vertebrates, serving comparable roles in steering, balance, and braking, unlike the unpaired dorsal, anal, and caudal fins.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The long and coiled intestine of a young tadpole is an adaptation to its
questions.explanation: Young tadpoles are primarily herbivorous, feeding on algae and plant material, which is comparatively harder to digest and lower in nutrients than animal protein — a long, coiled intestine provides the extra surface area and time needed for thorough digestion and absorption of this plant-based diet.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The major function of the swim-bladder in fishes is
questions.explanation: As established earlier, the swim bladder's main and most universal function across bony fishes is buoyancy control, allowing the fish to remain suspended at a particular depth without constant muscular effort.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which of the following animals has homodont dentition?
questions.explanation: The lizard has homodont dentition, meaning all its teeth are essentially the same shape, size, and function, unlike mammals such as rats and humans, which have heterodont dentition (different tooth types — incisors, canines, molars — specialized for different functions). Pigeons, being birds, have no teeth at all.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: In which of the following does external fertilization take place?
questions.explanation: Toads (and most amphibians) release their eggs and sperm directly into water, where fertilization occurs externally. Lizards, birds, and cockroaches all undergo internal fertilization within the female's body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The gill rakers of fishes take part in
questions.explanation: Gill rakers are comb-like projections on the gill arches that act as strainers, trapping food particles and preventing them from escaping through the gill slits back out of the mouth cavity — directly assisting in feeding, even though they are located on the respiratory gill structures.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct order of the development stages?
questions.explanation: Based on the diagram, frog/toad development proceeds from the fertilized egg through progressive tadpole stages toward the adult form in the specific sequence 5→3→2→1→4, matching the labelled stages shown in the source diagram.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Stage 3 breathes
questions.explanation: Based on the developmental sequence in the diagram, stage 3 corresponds to an early tadpole still possessing external gills, before these are later replaced by internal gills and eventually lungs as development proceeds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Cold blooded animals are referred to as
questions.explanation: "Poikilothermic" is the correct technical term for animals whose body temperature varies with their surrounding environment (cold-blooded animals), as opposed to "homoiothermic" (warm-blooded animals that maintain a constant internal temperature).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which of the organisms has lost the pentadactyl limb structure?
questions.explanation: The basic five-digit (pentadactyl) limb pattern, inherited from early tetrapod ancestors, has been entirely lost in fish, whose paired fins represent a more primitive limb form rather than a modified pentadactyl limb — unlike bats, frogs, and pigeons, whose wings/limbs are all clearly modified but still recognizably derived from the pentadactyl pattern.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which of the following combinations differentiates a bony fish from a cartilaginous fish? (I) Presence of gills (II) Absence of gill slits (III) Possession of bony skeleton (IV) Possession of a laterally compressed body (V) Possession of a dorso-ventrally compressed body
questions.explanation: Bony fish are specifically distinguished from cartilaginous fish by having their gill slits covered by an operculum (so gill slits are not individually visible externally — II), a skeleton made of true bone rather than cartilage (III), and typically a laterally compressed body shape (IV) — unlike cartilaginous fish (e.g. sharks), which have visible individual gill slits, a cartilage skeleton, and often a more dorso-ventrally flattened body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Which is the most important adaptation of a bony fish to life in water?

options.A: The possession of a streamlined shape
options.C: The covering of the body by a thin film of slime
options.D: The possession of a caudal fin

questions.explanation: A streamlined (fusiform) body shape is the single most fundamental adaptation for efficient aquatic life, dramatically reducing water resistance/drag as the fish swims — while scales, mucus/slime, and the caudal fin are all useful supporting adaptations, none is as fundamentally important as the overall streamlined body shape.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: In which of the following vertebrates does the skin function as a respiratory surface?
questions.explanation: The frog's moist, thin, well-vascularized skin is capable of significant gas exchange (cutaneous respiration), supplementing its lung breathing — a feature not typically shared by the drier or scaled skin of rats, lizards, or the gill-breathing skin of fish.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: In which of the following groups of vertebrates would the largest amount of yolk be found in the egg?
questions.explanation: Reptile eggs are laid on land and must sustain the full development of the embryo entirely within the shell (without additional external nourishment), requiring a comparatively very large yolk reserve — larger than the yolk typically found in fish or amphibian eggs, and far more than the minimal yolk in mammalian eggs, which instead receive nourishment directly from the mother via the placenta.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The structures that prevent food particles from escaping through the fish gills are called
questions.explanation: As covered earlier, gill rakers are the comb-like structures on the gill arches specifically responsible for straining out and retaining food particles, preventing them from being expelled with the outgoing respiratory water flow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The possession of scales, laying of eggs with shells and bony structure of the head are characteristics shared by
questions.explanation: Both reptiles and birds share scaly coverings (birds retain scales on their legs), lay shelled eggs, and have a bony skull structure — a combination of features reflecting their close evolutionary relationship (birds having evolved from reptilian ancestors).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The key event in the transition of the amphibians from water to land is the

options.A: replacement of the gills with lungs

questions.explanation: The single most critical adaptation enabling amphibians to move from an aquatic to a terrestrial existence is the replacement of gill-based respiration with lung-based breathing, allowing them to draw oxygen directly from air rather than relying on water for gas exchange.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The set of fins that controls steering, balancing and change of direction and pitch in fish is
questions.explanation: The paired pectoral and pelvic fins act analogously to limbs, providing the fine control needed for steering, balancing, and adjusting pitch (up/down tilt) as the fish swims, while the caudal fin mainly provides forward propulsion and the dorsal/anal fins mainly prevent rolling.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: Amphibians are normally found

options.A: on dry land and in water
options.B: in water and on moist land

questions.explanation: Amphibians characteristically lead a "double life" (the literal meaning of "amphibian"), requiring both an aquatic environment (especially for breeding and larval development) and moist land habitats (for their adult terrestrial activities), since their skin cannot tolerate prolonged dry conditions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The correct evolutionary sequence of the organisms represented is
questions.explanation: Vertebrate evolution proceeded in the well-established order: fish (earliest, fully aquatic) → amphibians (first to venture partly onto land) → reptiles (fully terrestrial, shelled eggs) → birds and mammals (most advanced, warm-blooded groups) — matching option A.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: The presence of endoskeleton is characteristic of
questions.explanation: An internal, bony or cartilaginous skeleton (endoskeleton) is the defining skeletal feature of vertebrates, in contrast to invertebrates such as insects (with an external chitinous exoskeleton) or coelenterates (with no rigid skeleton at all).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: A noticeable adaptation of the animal to its aquatic habitat is the possession of
questions.explanation: Webbed digits (feet) are a clear, direct structural adaptation that improves swimming efficiency by increasing the surface area pushed against the water with each stroke, making them a hallmark aquatic adaptation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.subcategory: CLASSIFICATION VI — VERTEBRATES I: PISCES, AMPHIBIANS, REPTILES
questions.question: (I) Rattus rattus (II) Agama agama (III) Bufo regularis (IV) Tilapia zilli. The order of evolutionary advancement of the above vertebrates is
